subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
When the house adjourned last night I was discusing with the minister a certain provision of this bill, and calling attention to the fact that he had at different times in the course of the discussion stated that the object of the previous government in appointing trustees for a fixed term was to tie the hands of a succeeding government, and when I made that statement the minister replied, "So it was," as will be found at page 3422 of Hansard. Then I said:
I ask the minister to read the report of the Duff commission and to study the reason why that commission recommended the appointment of a board of trustees and recommended also that it be given permanence.
At the time I did not have before me the report of the Duff commission, and I now call the minister's attention to clause 204 of that report, which says in part:
One of the trustees should be named as chairman at the date of his appointment with tenure of office seven years.
The minister surely does not think that away back behind the report of this commission the government set out with or was able to impose upon that commission a desire to tie the hands of its successor. In answer to the request of the minister as to why the recommendation of the Duff commission as to the length of tenure of office was not followed, I said I was not sure. The appointment of the chairman was made for a term of five years instead of seven, again disclosing an absence of all desire on the part of the previous government to tie the hands of a succeeding government for any particular period of time. The report of the commission discloses certain conditions with which the minister is familiar, political interference in the management of the road and extravagance in its management, all of which is specifically set out in the report, and has been referred to at different times in this debate.
I really think, Mr. Chairman, that the minister ought to withdraw the statement that it was the intention of the government to tie the hands of its successor, when the fact is that an honest and sincere effort was made to carry out the recommendation of this very important, impartial and capable commission, and that was all that was behind the appointment of the board of trustees. I would ask the minister if he still persists in the statement that the object of the government was to tie the hands of its successors.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I am sorry to have to differ from my hon. friend. I do not think I can withdraw my statement. It seems to me that when the. term of office was being considered and a change was being made from the recommendation of the Duff report, it could have been for a term within the life of the parliament then sitting. I think that would have been wiser. That is all I have to say about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
It is quite obvious that the term was to preserve continuity, for one of the trustees was to leave office next fall, another next year, and in two years more the chairman would retire; but it was thought that seven years was too long, and so the term was made five years. In the debate which took place it was quite clear that the whole bill was framed on the Duff report, and for the minister to suggest improper motives is not only contravening the rules of the house but is not in accordance with the facts. The term of office was lessened for the very purpose of meeting unfair criticism that the hands of the next parliament were being tied by the then parliament. When a grant was being given to the federal commission of this city I argued that we should not go beyond the life of a particular parliament, but the Prime Minister took the other view.
Public interest is not always synonymous with pure partyism. It does not mean that, and if it is impossible for hon. gentlemen opposite to conceive of other people having an honest desire to carry into effect the report of the Duff commission, merely because they want now to remove the trustees who were promised a certain term of office, they have no right to attribute improper motives to those who sincerely endeavoured to give effect to the recommendations of the commission appointed, not at the instance of any one railway, but at the instance of both, because both railways thought it desirable in the public interest that such a report should be made.

Paragraph agreed to.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
May I ask if the minister
would be so kind as to give us a clear statement as to the differences between the powers of the board of directors as proposed under this bill and the powers of the trustees treated by the act of 1933? I have puzzled my brain over it but I cannot see very much difference between the powers of the directors as stated in these sections and the powers of the trustees as they were created by the act of 1933.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I thought my hon. friend saw a very decided difference, because he claimed that one made for an improvement all round and the other led to unlimited graft and corruption.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I still adhere to that opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
There is a difference, and I
will try to explain it. First there is no difference in this principle, that the management of the internal affairs of the Canadian National Railways is now vested in the hands of the trustees, and under this bill will be vested in the hands of the board of directors. But at the present time those powers are vested in one man, who must agree to every action that is taken respecting the internal affairs of the Canadian National Railways-one man in charge of a property far-flung from coast to coast, and of the magnitude of the Canadian National Railways. In addition, that one man is operating some eight departments of the railway directly. In other words, he is not only running all the affairs of the railway personally but he is acting as the manager of eight departments of the railway. He has two co-trustees, neither of whom can carry out anything that is suggested unless the chairman agrees, and always one must agree with the chairman to make a particular act effective. That is the present set-up.
Under the new set-up we have a chairman. He is one member of the board of directors, and he will have six other directors with him of the type described in the Duff commission's report, if it is possible to get them-and I am satisfied that it is-men of experience in financial matters and with a background in the industrial life of Canada which will permit them to make an important contribution to the affairs of the railway. We have in this case a full time chairman as was the case with the board of trustees. The chairman of the board of trustees was assisted by two part time directors; in this case, by six. When the seven sit around the table each will have an equal vote in deciding any matter of policy coming before the board. That is the main difference.
There is no difference so far as outside control goes. The present board of trustees have 
to go to the government with respect to certain matters in .which the government and railroad are so interlocked that it is impossible for one to act without the other. The new board will be in the same position, and the contact will be between a practical railway man as chairman and the Minister of Railways. The contact at present is between the chairman of the board of trustees, who is not a railroad man at all, and who must necessarily bring an adviser with him. Present discussions between the Minister of Railways and any practical railway man is conducted through a third party, who has no first hand knowledge of most matters under discussion but who must convey the views of the practical railway man to the government. Those are the main differences, and I think they are very important.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
But what supervision will
the Minister of Railways have over the proceedings of the directors? I do not think, simply because the chairman of trustees had supervision over several departments of the railway, that that is altogether a crime, as the extravagance and emphasis of the language of the minister would seem to indicate. When the new Department of Transport is set up I assume the hon. gentleman will preside over it. He will then have the supervision and direction of several departments or branches. If the employees in that new department are to be appointed outside of the civil service, he will have a direct voice in the appointment of more persons than any previous minister has had in the history of Canada. If he considers himself qualified for the supervision of so many branches, I cannot understand why he should think the chairman of trustees is so absolutely disqualified. He has admitted himself that he has been unable to find any serious error of act or judgment which could be charged against the present board of trustees or the chairman of the board. The hon. gentleman has put himself out of court by admitting that he can find no real cause for criticism.
He has suggested that Mr. Fullerton is disqualified because he was not trained as a railway man. I call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that he himself is not a railway man. The other great competing railroad is in charge of a gentleman of high qualifications and large experience, but he was not originally a railway man. I could take the minister to many of the leading corporations in the United States where the great executive heads are not trained in the mechanical operations which are carried on by the particular corporation

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
over which they preside. A gentleman with whom I have been intimate since his youth is the executive head of the General Electric Company of the United States. He is merely a lawyer; he never was a railway man or a manufacturer. It is quite possible for a man who is not a railway man to act as chairman of the board of trustees and supervise and direct affairs in such a manner as to preserve and maintain the best interests of the public service over which he is placed. Are the members of this new board of directors to be railway men? Are they to be selected because of their railroading experience?
Except in one instance, the hon. gentleman has not been able to indicate any difference between the powers and responsibilities of these directors and the powers and responsibilities of the trustees. The chairman of the board of trustees had to have the concurrence of one of the other two trustees, and the other two could not carry out matters of policy except with the consent of the chairman. The so-called departments over which the chairman had supervision were not departments connected with the actual running and operation of the railway system. The more I think of this the more I am driven to the conclusion that the purport of the bill is to change by statute a board of trustees into a board of directors, the appointment to which will rest with the hon. gentleman and depend upon his recommendation and selection. I am driven to the conclusion that the whole purpose of the bill is to obtain for the minister political control over the management, maintenance and operation of every department of the railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member referred to supervision by the chairman over certain departments. The fact is that the chairman is operating manager of seven or eight departments, in addition to running the whole show as chairman. I want to make that clear, because there is a slight difference. The hon. gentleman said that my department would be the largest in Canada, but I ask him to compare it with the Canadian National Railways. When this new department is formed there will be some 5,000 employees in it, but there are over 75,000 in the Canadian National Railways. I will be in charge of property valued at only one-twenty-fifth or one-thirtieth the value of the property of the Canadian National Railways. I admit I have a very difficult task; it is perhaps an open question whether too much work will not be connected with this department, but the
hon. member was comparing two totally dissimilar things. It might be true to say that the chairman, not being a qualified railway man, has a task somewhat beyond his capacity, and that I, not being a qualified railway man, have a task somewhat beyond mine, but it would not be for the same reason.
I think we had better straighten out the question as to what this government is trying to do. The impression has been created that we are passing this bill to dismiss three trustees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: That is what you said.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: We are passing this legislation to get a better set-up for the Canadian National Railway. When I first took office I talked with the trustees individually and each told me that the present set-up is bad. I talked with my predecessor in office, and he said it was bad. I heard the views of other people who had had close experience with the situation, and they felt it was impossible. Just how far should the personality of the chairman be allowed to intrude into this matter? I think it has gone rather a long way. A few days ago in the committee on railways and shipping the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) demanded that the chairman be given the privilege of making a statement. Objection was raised because this bill was not before the committee, but I took the view that I should like to see the chairman have his day in court if he so desired. I saw nothing behind it at all; I thought it was only fair that he should be given this opportunity. He came before the committee and made his statement. I thought it was a very fair statement, and I made some rather flattering remarks about it. But what happened? A beautiful document-I understand it has been published both in English and in French-is being flooded over the country, being a reprint of the chairman's statement.

country. That is all I care to say. We believe that in the interests of the railway a change should be made.
If there should be any hardship imposed upon the chairman by this change, I am quite prepared to see that he does not suffer financially. There is nothing personal in the relations existing between the chairman and myself. The chairman happens to be involved in this change, and I am sorry. I did my best to see that his personality would not be involved when the time for reorganization came, but the fact remains that I believe it is necessary in the interests of the railway to change this system of management. That is the view of the government. Why pound away on the individuality of a man who happens to be chairman of the board?

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
in office with respect to the matter. The minister persists in stating or insinuating or suggesting that the object behind the fixing of the period of office of the trustees was a political one; that it was done for the purpose of tying the hands of a succeeding government.

This comes from the Minister of Railways and it comes after long consideration, and is repeated; this is the second or third time he has made that statement. I ask the Minister of Finance, who is
questioning motives? I referred to the record and showed that the recommendations of the Duff commission embodied the appointment of a board of trustees for a longer period of office than the one for which they were appointed. Surely therefore that destroys entirely the contention, oft repeated in this house by the Minister of Railways, that the motive of the former government was to tie the hands of a succeeding government. I asked the minister to withdraw it but he declined to do so. So he reaffirms it. The record is against him. Not only is the record against him on that, but it is against him on other matters he has stated to-day. He says that the chairman of the board of trustees took over the charge of operating departments of the road.

When in the world did it become out of order for the chairman of any organization in charge of the national railways to make a statement in explanation of his conduct or in justification of it? Whenever did it become out of order? It never has been, and, I hope, never will be. However, here is what the chairman said:
I now turn to the departments which came under my direct management. Section 10 of the 1933 act provides:-
"The trustees shall appoint, on terms to be fixed by them, and with the titular rank of president, a person other than one of themselves to execute and perform, under and in consultation with them, the powers, authorities and duties of chief operating officer of national railways, as such powers, authorities and duties shall be from time to time defined by by-law or resolution of the trustees and committed for execution and performance. The president shall report and be responsible to the trustees and to them alone."
That is in a statute passed by this parliament. The chairman continues:
It is my view that the person who fills this position has a task requiring not only high technical skill, but demanding his full time and attention. On January 31, 1934, the trustees appointed Mr. S. J. Hungerford as chief operating officer. In arranging the division of departments between the president and myself I took over those departments which were not connected with the actual operation of the railway. Those connected with the operation of the railway proper were assigned to the president, and I have never at any time interfered in their operation,

although I recognize that the ultimate responsibility for the efficiency of those operations rests with the board. The working out of this arrangement has been harmonious and I have never heard of any complaint from any railway officer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Paragraph 9 makes the
shareholders of the company the governor in council and the governor in council the shareholders of the company for all purposes that
C.NJt.-Board of Directors

may require the consent of the shareholders. That is, where under any statute, including the railway act or the railway commission act, it is necessary for the consent of shareholders to be given, the governor in council acts as such shareholders. That of course is a wide extension of the powers which have heretofore been exercised in th-t regard. I suppose yesterday when dealing with this matter the minister intended to point out what successive ministers have pointed out, namely that here we have a system which, if it were a private one, would be in the hands of receivers. There can be no argument as to their having defaulted in payment of interest on their securit' s, and under those circumstances a receive.- would be appointed by the courts and the lines would be operated by the receivers. It is conceivable that a possible difficulty might arise. For instance, Canadian Northern British Columbia bonds are guaranteed by the province of British Columbia. If we did not pay interest on those bonds, the province of British Columbia could not do it. The same is true with respect to Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The same is also true in connection with the Halifax and Southwestern no"way in Nova Scotia. These facts have a pertinent bearing upon the whole situation. I have expressed and do now express surprise that the minister is not dealing with that phase of it. It was that which influencd the commission in support of the judgment which I read when I spoke in the debate on second reading. If this were a private enterprise it would be operated by receivers, and they would issue receivers' certificates which they would sell for the purpose of obtaining fresh capital, in the meantime not paying any interest upon the securities, but rather accumulating against the day of reorganization. Under those circumstances the trustees were appointed, and those trustees to which the irinistc. referred yesterday. because of the financial position of the railways, occupied a very special position. To sub titute directors must have the effect to which attention has so often been directed in this chamber, and which I shall not deal with at this time.
Now we come to the finding of fresh capital. The old act provided that that principle should be maintained and that the government would find fresh capital. Why? Because the property being in the condition in which it is, fresh capital must be found or it will not be found at all. For it they obtained receivers' certificates in the form of securities of the railway itself. That is, I assume the securities of the railways are being accumulated from one secur-

ity payment, one promise to pay. The commission recommended that instead of issuing securities of the railways guaranteed by the government, thereafter the security should be issued by the government and the money loaned by the government to the railways. So that part of the debt that has been accumulated over the last five years, I think something like twenty per cent of the whole, is Canadian National debt. Under preceding administrations that was not so; the debt was the debt of the Canadian National, guaranteed by the country, and the securities were securities sold by the railway company. The change was for one purpose, to effect economy, and to bring home to the people the realities of the situation. It was believed by the Duff commission, and especially by those who had to do with the financial side of the railway, that if parliament had from year to year to find the money and make it a direct charge against the people themselves they would be more interested in the enterprise; the principle of the enterprise that was unable to meet its fixed charges would be maintained right through the whole administrative process, namely, trustees, capital provided by the government, not at the will of the trustees but at the will of the government, and if they did not think the case made out by the trustees was sufficient they would not, as investors would not in the case of a company in the hands of a receiver, advance the money for capital expenditures. But the deficit, and that is where the whole point comes in, would have to be paid by the people. Why? Because default in the payment of interest on a guaranteed security has the same effect upon the credit of this country as failure to pay interest on its direct obligations. That is what differentiates this whole enterprise from an ordinary enterprise that is failing to pay its fixed charges. If it were not for that, the situation would be very simple; but once we put our guarantee behind all these securities we must pay them or default, and if we default our credit is gone, alike with respect to direct and indirect obligations.
Now we have said that where the assent of the shareholders is required, and it will be recalled that for purposes of borrowing the consent of the shareholders is sometimes required to be expressed in a given way, that shall be done by the governor in council. I suppose that is the easiest and simplest way in which the matter can be done, but it involves the acceptance of a very strange principle by those who formerly so vigorously opposed such powers being conferred upon

C.N.R.-Board o/ Directors
the governor in council. The real difficulty we have always had in this and other countries is to know who will represent the shareholders in a publicly owned enterprise. Yesterday the Minister of Finance was stating he had some plans in his mind as to how to select the directors. I have gone over the matter on several occasions in various ways, hoping to bring a sense of responsibility more directly home to the people, but we have not done it.
The government of the country cannot say that it represents the shareholders, because the shareholders are all the people in all the provinces, and of all shades of political opinion. It may well be that the heaviest shareholders, being those who pay the largest taxes, by reason of conditions, may not be interested in any political party at all. Under these circumstances the powers conferred are very great, but I suppose the answer the minister will give is that this is the simplest way in which to deal with it. It is always simple, I suppose; but I used to be told in this house in days gone by that to confer powers of this kind upon the executive was a departure from the well established rules of constitutional government. Be that as it may, what we are doing here is to say that wherever under the provisions of the railway act or any other statute approval by the shareholders has to be given under the law, and there are numerous cases once you take away the trustees, in all such oases "with respect to any company to which the next preceding section applies, such approval, sanction or confirmation may be given by the governor in council." That means all the subsidiaries. 139 in number, because it will be found in the letter that was signed by Mr. Liddy that the Canadian National comprises 139 companies, as stated in evidence; the Canadian Pacific conducts its own affiliated operations through approximately the same number of companies, and in the case of all these 139 subsidiaries the shareholders will find themselves in the position of votes being given by the governor in council exercising shareholders' rights, and they are not all of them companies of which we are the complete owners. But we are providing that all these affiliated companies shall be represented by the governor in council regardless of whether they have provincial or federal incorporation. I question the legality of it, to start with, and in the second place I think it is an unprecedented exercise of executive authority. It confers on the governor in council power to represent shareholders in provincial companies, whether the shareholders are in complete control of the
road or not. For instance, the Central Vermont Railway is a road in which the Canadian National has a very large interest. We were told at one time we would not incur any responsibility in the rehabilitation' of that system. What happened was that it issued its securities, which were put in the treasury of the Canadian National, and then this country guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian National Railway which were sold on the markets of the world and provided the money. So we have a vital interest in that system. The Canadian National, I understand, has a substantial holding in that road. The Central Vermont would probably not come within the operation of this section because it does not run into Canada, but there is a road that crosses the boundary and runs partly into Canada as a continuous line, namely, the Grand Trunk Western, which crosses via the St. Clair tunnel under the river, running on the rails of the tunnel company, the tunnel company being a separate company, with part of the tunnel in the United States and part of it in Canada. All these are matters of such importance that it is a very serious matter to declare that regardless of every other consideration the governor in council shall represent the shareholders of all these companies whenever approval has to be given, or in the language of the section:
Whenever under the provisions of the Railway Act or any other statute or law the approval, sanction or confirmation by shareholders is required with respect to any company to which the next preceding section applies,-
That is, any one of the affiliated companies. -such approval, sanction or confirmation may be given by the governor in council.
This bill declares that the present officers are relieved of their duties and the new directors shall be the directors of the enterprise, and it is provided in the preceding section that:
The National Act and all statutes, charters, letters patent and orders in council of Canada which relate to any of such companies in Canada shall, in so far as they may be inconsistent with the provisions of this section, be read in the light hereof and be construed so as to conform herewith.
Not only is this an extraordinary power, but I greatly fear it is a wholly illegal power applied to some at least of the companies in question.

speechtext:
That is what I had reference to. Read alone the preceding section might not be important, but when this section and later sections are read with it, they certainly confer wider powers than we have ever undertaken to confer in this country. Paragraph 9 reads:
Whenever under the provisions of the Railway Act or any other statute or law the approval, sanction or confirmation by shareholders is required with respect to any company to which the next preceding section applies, such approval, sanction or confirmation may be given by the governor in council.
What we have done is to take the provincial companies and make them into federal incorporations willy-nilly. Then we have said that the new directors shall become directors of those companies willy-nilly. Then we have said that if there are more than seven, a certain method is to be followed for the purpose of selecting them. Then we say that any statute, charter, lease or whatever it may be that is inconsistent with the provisions of the section, shall be read in the light thereof and be construed so as to conform therewith. That in itself is a tremendous exercise of power. In the main, that power was conferred by the act we are amending, but in that case the trustees represented the shareholders as well as the security holders. That was the whole basis of the report made by the commission, and it was for that very reason that they went so carefully into the financial set-up of the enterprise. The minute we earn enough money to pay the interest on the securities, it is quite clear that the statute would be amended, but as long as the conditions exist to which reference has been made, there will be a situation entirely different from the one the minister contemplates.
What he now says is that they are going to treat this company as a company which is meeting the obligations of its fixed charges from year to year. Treating it as such, the

governor in council becomes a shareholder, not only for the purposes of the company but for the purposes of the subsidiaries as well. That is an entirely different thing from what prevailed in the case of the trustees. They represented the shareholders. As the minister knows, in an ordinary legal proceeding receivers are officers of the court, and the trustees were officers of the high court of parliament. The shareholders have no longer anything to say when receivers are appointed, and will not have anything to say until the system is reorganized and they once more come into the authority of their position. What we are doing by this legislation is to say that the company no longer occupies that position, whereas we are to deal with legislation at this very session which indicates that we shall have to raise from $35,000,000 to $40,000,000 to pay the interest upon the securities. There is a contradiction between the two. The one is logical and consistent, the other is illogical and inconsistent; the one is contradictory and the other is selfexplanatory. That is the real truth about it. I direct attention to it, but I know there is no likelihood of its being changed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and it seems to me that the statements that have been made during the second reading of this bill were made by hon. gentlemen opposite in an effort to show that the Canadian National Railways is not worth a cent to this country which is burdened down with debt. An effort has been made to show a conflict between the act of 1919, the act incorporating the various companies that go to make up the Canadian National system, the trustee act of 1933 and the present bill as introduced by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Howe). I desire to state as emphatically as I can that if there is connected with the Canadian National railway system any piece of road which is not paying-I refer particularly to the Canadian Northern- it was placed in the system by whom? Was it by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)? Was it by his late lamented leader, Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier? No, it was by a fellow Nova Scotian, the Right Hon. Sir Robert Laird Borden. He took over the Canadian Northern to save

C.N.R..-Board of Directors
the Bank of Commerce. He gave them $40,000,000 for the Canadian Northern and then appointed a commission to find out the amount of the equity of redemption of Mackenzie and Mann. This royal commission found they were entitled to receive $10,000,000. At the very inception of this system the country was saddled with a piece of railway which should have been put up for sale under the hammer. This was a private corporation and it should have been sold for what it was worth to any one who desired to buy it.
The leader of the opposition referred to the Halifax and Southwestern Railway. As the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has just indicated, that railroad was built under a provincial charter. The province paid subsidies of $3,400 per mile. This railroad was taken into the Canadian National system. I cannot lay my hand upon it at the moment, but the previous government, I believe in 1932, stated that the Intercolonial Railway should consist of those roads in Nova Scotia which belonged to Mackenzie and Mann and that the Halifax and Southwestern should become part of the Intercolonial system, as it was known up to the time it was handed over under the legislation of Sir Robert Laird Borden. Under the legislation of 1919, which came into effect in 1922, the Grand Trunk in the United States and in Canada became part of the Canadian National Railway. The Intercolonial, which was owned by the government as trustees for the people and which was built as a term of confederation, as covered by section 145 of the British North America Act, was also brought into the system.
The leader of the opposition, the former Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), who came from Nova Scotia and now lives in Montreal, and other hon. gentlemen opposite, have testified that they had no relationship with Mr. Fullerton or the other directors. One by one they have come and told us that: I met him in the rotunda of the hotel and I bowed to him, but that was all. I suppose if he stays long enough they will be able to turn things over in their minds and discover whether or not he winked at them. The leader of the opposition, and the gentlemen who support him in this house are doing everything they can to frustrate the policies of this government and of the people with respect to the operation of the Canadian National system, and when you begin to raise doubts in the minds of the people that the securities that are outstanding are securities that may not be worth the paper they are written on, notwithstanding that the railways to-day are owned by the people and
12730-210J
have the people behind them, it is just another evidence of the campaign of propaganda that started somewhere in the city of Montreal and has been pursued every week, in leaflet and in pamphlet, in reference to the management and the condition of the system. And that has been carried on-I ask hon. gentlemen opposite to refute this-for no other purpose than to hand over the Canadian National system to Sir Edward Beatty and the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Let us have a clear understanding of this matter. I speak not only as a member of this house but as one who has had some experience in the public life of the country and of his own province, and I say this afternoon that my whole life as a public man has been devoted to the best interests of the people and of their future. As I said in the house last night, I may not live long-I do not expect to-but I think it is the first duty of every hon. gentleman, including the leader of the opposition, with the power and knowledge that he possesses, to support the will of the people and to assist rather than oppose the government in the tremendous task which they have to perform with respect to our national railways. H the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier had taken over the system the responsibility would be upon this side of the house to-day; if the present Prime Minister had taken it over, the responsibility would be his. But when I look opposite I see sitting there to-day hon. gentlemen who were in this house when that legislation was passed in the days of Sir Robert Laird Borden and of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. I wonder whether my hon. friends ever stop to think that if the Canadian National system is in the condition in which it is said to be-and I do not know exactly what that condition is -the condition is due absolutely to the fact that the Conservative government of Sir Robert Borden took over the railways. And I speak of Sir Robert Borden with great respect, for he comes from my own province; indeed, I studied law in the same city with him and was often in his office in the days when I was beginning to take up the profession. It is not fair to place the responsibility upon the present Minister of Railways or upon the Prime Minister of the day.
The point I want to make quite clear is that legislation will have to be brought down-and this is a suggestion to the government made in the open-not at this session but after they have had an opportunity of looking into the matter and have obtained advice from their legal advisers, to deal satisfactorily with the Intercolonial railway, so that the Intercolonial shall remain as it was when it was completed under Sir Wilfrid Laurier, with the various
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

branches that were built up as subsidiaries. To-day we find the Halifax and Southwestern, which belonged to the Canadian Northern and in which we put S3,400 a mile, as part of the Intercolonial railway, though it has no more right to be a part of the Intercolonial railway than I can claim to belong to the country from which Haile Selassie had to flee, seeking protection as a guest of the people of England. I say to the leader of the opposition that these are matters of great importance. The Grand Trunk Pacific was built under Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and so was the Transcontinental-for what purpose? It was for the purpose of bringing the maritime provinces closer to the great centres of Canada. It was built at a time when everyone believed that the twentieth century belonged to Canada. But a great war broke out, a war in which Canada took part, in which her noble sons fought and died that civilization might continue and that we might have the liberties that we have always enjoyed under the great British constitution. Following that came the great slump of 1929, from which Canada has not yet recovered. Immigration had to stop. But such were the knowledge and the vision of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his cabinet in days gone by that if their intentions had been carried out, and if the war had not taken place, if the great depression of 1929 had not overtaken us, our Canadian west to-day would be filled and there would probably be a population of twenty or twenty-five million people in this country. Unfortunately however these vast areas in the west are not being tilled to the extent to which they might be, and ten million people have to carry the tremendous financial responsibility.
In these circumstances it seems to me hon. gentlemen opposite do not offer to the government even constructive criticism; their criticism is all destructive. They do not support the government in the task which it has to perform. I have no doubt that we all love our country; I do not believe that love of country is all on this side of the house; there is as much over there as there is here. But there seems to be some sinister motive on the outside, as evidenced in these pamphlets and in the propaganda that is being carried on and is seeping through the cracks and crevices of this chamber, to discourage the people of Canada with respect to the Canadian National Railways. The Prime Minister and his cabinet have undertaken to restore to the system a board of directors such as Sir Robert Borden provided for as the proper method of managing the railways. As the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen said in this house, there is no other system, no other management in connection with the Canadian National Railways than a

board of directors; for, as he pointed out, the interests of the country are diversified and what is suitable to one section does not suit another. Therefore, in order to keep the system as far as possible out of politics, Sir Robert Borden provided for a board possessing a knowledge of the varied interests with which they were concerned, a board made up of gentlemen who understood the conditions that existed in the different parts of the country from which they came. Was Sir Robert Laird Borden wrong? Was the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen wrong? And is the only man who is right on this great question to-day the present leader of the opposition? If that is so he is at opposite points to his predecessors in office and to the very honourable gentlemen who gave this system, not as it is to-day, but largely so, to the country, to be brought to fruition through the years. I have none but the friendliest feeling towards hon. gentlemen opposite, and I think that when in their quiet moments they sit down and reflect upon their position they will realize that what was perhaps the hardest fought campaign the Conservative party ever contested in this country was lost from the beginning, that the leader of the opposition knew he was fighting a losing battle, and though he put his best foot forward, defeat perched on his banner; but on that account they need not despair; they need despair only if hon. gentlemen continue in a carping way to belittle the purposes of the present government in trying to put this Canadian National Railway system on its feet, and to refuse the support that is due to the Prime Minister, or if not to the Prime Minister, to the government, or if not to the government and the hon. gentlemen who sit on this side of the house, to the people of this country.
My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition and those associated with him represent a large number of electors. To them I say, in concluding my observations at this time, that under the trustee act as introduced by my right hon. friend in 1933 it was evident that he cared not for the rights of anybody in this country except three classes enumerated in the statute who might possibly succeed in obtaining damages by virtue of their relationship to the Canadian National Railways. But in reference to every other statute, to every other right, to everything that was sacred because it was the property of the people, that legislation was seriously defective. Why, sir, there is contained in that statute a clause to the effect that the railways may, if they so desire, tear up the tracks, cease to operate the trains, and do away with roads that the people have paid for-all subject only to the railway

C.NJt.-Board of Directors
commission of Canada. Is that commission the last word in this country? Is it the only body that can decide these things? Is it the body that should have the right to tell the people of Canada and this parliament and this government: You have nothing in the world to do with the railways? There was placed on the statute books of this country, when my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition was Prime Minister, the clause which enabled either privately owned or publicly owned companies to tear up their tracks and stop the use of their roads for public purposes if the railway commission of Canada permitted them so to do. Are the hands of this parliament tied with reference to the matter of who should be the manager of this road? This government is taking a leaf out of the book of Sir Robert Laird Borden and the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who said that for the Canadian National Railways the directorate system was the proper one, the system best suited to the needs of this great country, extending as it does from the Atlantic to the Pacific, including nine provinces with differing aspirations, but desiring only one object, the success of this vast confederation. These distinguished men having said that the directorate system was the best, and my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition having said, in the act of 1933, that it was not, he will have to go into the house of his friends and settle that question with them, not with hon. members who sit on this side of the house and who have a direct mandate from the people to place upon the statute books a measure returning to the system of directorates, and to give a fair trial to the new administration in its endeavour to make that railway what the people of Canada desire it to be, a railway that will conduce to the prosperity of all parts of the dominion, and make happy and contented those who will come after us, if not we ourselves. In my humble opinion these are the considerations that should actuate criticism on the part of the right hon. leader of the opposition and his supporters, and which require that it should be constructive.
Midway between his assumption of office as Prime Minister and his exit from the political stage in that capacity, he placed upon the statute books in 1933 the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act. That, to use his own words, was rather telling, rather significant, and I ask him now why it was, when he was going to do away with the president and the board of directors and substitute a board of trustees, he did not do that
by itself as a distinct piece of legislation rather than mix it up in a conglomeration of paragraphs that occupy many pages of the statute books, between the railway commission, the Canadian National, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk, and the Intercolonial Railway provisions. Those things are all intermixed in that statute of 1933, although it was the right and the privilege of the leader of the opposition to have remedied that state of things if in his judgment it was the proper thing to do. It should have been distinct and apart from other ramifications in reference to very many matters that have no direct relationship to the question of the board of trustees and its management of the Canadian National railway system.
Under the act of 1933, and dealing with the subparagraph of which the leader of the opposition has been speaking, I cannot for the life of me see why it was that they were so determined not only to nail their party interests to the cross, but the people of Canada also, who have to carry the financial burdens. I do not understand why they made it so hard for the present government, representatives of the people, with the largest majority ever given to any party since Can ada became a confederation. The Prime Minister of to-day, then leader of the opposition, said in the city of Toronto that he wanted a verdict from the people, he wanted a clear mandate, he wanted them to understand that if he came back to office this act of 1933 must go by the board and a new system of management and control of the Canadian National Railways must come into effect. I heard his voice over the radio in the city of Halifax, when he spoke to that vast audience in Massey Hall, Toronto. Surely if he was.fair enough, and, as he always has been, honourable enough, to make known to the people of this country what his policy was going to be, after it has been endorsed so unmistakably there should be no question about our putting through this measure. The people have endorsed that policy so strongly that there is not room on this side of the house for all hon. members who support the Prime Minister. Some of them have to sit on the other side and associate with the right hon. leader of the opposition; sometimes people think they belong to his party, but they do not.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say the mandate of the people comes ahead of the statute of 1933 and it is the duty of parliament and the government to implement the pledges then given to the people of this country. That is what has been done, in bringing down this

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
legislation and placing the control of the Canadian National Railways back in the hands of the people through a board of directors subject to the control of parliament, the representatives of the people. Surely no one can say that is not standing behind constitutional government and the very finest conceptions of democracy. President Wilson wanted to make the world safe for democracy. It seems to me that the harder the right hon. Prime Minister tried to make Canada safe for democracy the more hon. gentlemen opposite, led by my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, try to remove the foundations of our democratic thought, our democratic principles, our constitutional ideas, which have been behind England's success through the years and which have built up the British empire which to-day is as free as the sun and which will remain free as long as the people live within the law and the proper authorities place that law upon the statute books in the various countries.
I make this statement, Mr. Chairman, only because I feel that the people of Canada should know that this propaganda has succeeded in getting into this very chamber. Last night my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George said there was another chamber making up this parliament, namely the senate, and we had to deal with them. I should like nothing better than to go to the people of my own constituency-and I would do it tomorrow-if the senate dared to turn down this legislation as it has been introduced in this house and as it will be passed by this house, representing the will of the people. If that is done, some day in the near future they will find that the door will be locked and they will not be able to get in. I remember that the ex-Minister of Finance, who I regret is ill, locked the door on the legislative council in the province of Nova Scotia, and said, "You have no rights or privileges. Go home and attend to your business, but keep away from here." Did they talk about indemnities, those people who were appointed for life? No, sir, they did not.
But those are not democratic ways of doing things; they are autocratic; they seem to be the ways of some hon. gentlemen who sit opposite. They are not followed by the present Prime Minister, who is simple in his love for Canada, who carries nothing but the best thoughts for everyone. If I had any criticism of the right hon. gentleman at all it would be that he is too generous, too kind. He has too broad an outlook as to the future of this country, and his main desire is to see that the policies he believes best are carried out so that the people of Canada may have

at least a little time in which to go ahead and enjoy more of the prosperity that ceased when the bell rang in 1911 on reciprocity. Then we heard "no truck or trade with the Yankees," but a few years later we saw hon. gentlemen opposite, when in power, taking a different view and going off to Washington in an endeavour to negotiate a reciprocity pact. It is a good thing that ex-President Taft of the United States was not alive and in office at that time, or my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition might have been asked to withdraw the statement made by his party that they would have no truck or trade with the Yankees. He might have been told, "Take your bag home; carry it yourself. There is nothing to be put in it."
Ah, Mr. Chairman, these are the things for the public to remember. These are the things that sink deep into the hearts of men. The position taken by the Prime Minister is the sort of thing that makes for better government and for better relationship between the different parties in this house. That is not done by creating in the public mind a feeling of unrest with regard to this national railway system. We have, this system; we have to deal with it, and we are going to keep it, in spite of Sir Edward Beatty's public statement in Canada and in London that, notwithstanding the parliament of Canada and the will of the people, within three years the Canadian National would be associated with the Canadian Pacific, of which he is the president. Whoever gave him the right to make that statement? He must have had someone standing nearby who gave him the impression that there was some possibility of bringing about such a thing. He has a great railway system. In the early days his company received the very best soil in our Canadian west, and the people of this country contributed large sums of money for the construction of that road. To-day they, or those they have brought to this country, are in possession of that land, and the Canadian Pacific is receiving thousands and thousands of dollars from the grants of land and as a result of the financial support given that company by the parliament of Canada in the early days of confederation. I say to Sir Edward Beatty that if he will attend to the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Prime Minister, the government, this house and the people of Canada will attend to the Canadian National system. It belongs to the people, not to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
May I say, Mr. Chairman, that it is a very nice compliment to me that, when I am speaking in the interests of the people of this country, the hon. member for St.

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
Lawrence-St. George should leave the chamber and the right hon. leader of the opposition should cross the floor to enter into a discussion wTh the Minister of Justice, because he cannot stand the gaff. It is a sort of lefthanded compliment to the senior or junior- I don't know which I am-member for Halifax. I want to say to him that he has been handed so many left-handed compliments by the people of Canada that it does not hurt him to hand him one more. I shall close my eyes as if in oblivion to his passing from that side to this, because I believe in my heart he likes this side better than that. If there is any enjoyment in what he has done I am pleased; I am made very happy. With that I shall stop before the gong rings.
Paragraph 9 agreed to.

May I have permission to clear up a matter about which there was some difficulty this afternoon. I now have before me the proceedings of the standing committee on railways and shipping. At page 208 I find the following:
Hon. Mr. Howe: I might say, Mr. Stewart, that the trustees have already made two annual statements. No one is preventing them from making any statement at any time or in any place they like. Why insist that they make a statement before this particular committee to which this bill has not been referred? They can make a statement in the newspapers if they want to.
Hon. Mr. Stewart: I say that this is the proper place to investigate matters relating to the Canadian National Railways. The press is not the place. This committee should be the place in which to get the facts.
It was a statement by the minister, not by the chairman of the committee.
On section 3, paragraph 10-appointment of president.

Paragraph 10 provides a salary for the president when he acts as chief executive officer. This was to take care of providing a salary for the chairman and president. A careful reading suggests that it might be interpreted that he was being paid
two salaries, one as chief executive officer and the other as president. We find that without these words he will be sure of his salary, and for these reasons they are superfluous.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Speaking to the amendment and to the section I suppose the minister will agree that to no inconsiderable extent success or failure will be determined by the president of the system. The hon. gentleman will recall that it was because of difficulties in connection with that situation that this country sought a president from outside Canada. He will also recall that the London and North Eastern Railway sought and obtained a chief executive officer in the United States, in the person of the late Sir Henry Thornton. In my judgment the whole question as to the present situation of the Canadian National Railways requires immediate attention. If the minister had known, perhaps he would not have used the terms he did as to the possibility of trustees being in conference with me with respect to administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Because I have differed materially about some things. However, that is not the issue. There is in the Canadian National at Montreal in my judgment-and I say this with great hesitancy, and am giving my opinion-a clique-and I do not use the word in an offensive sense-that makes it impossible to accomplish certain things which must be accomplished, if the system is to succeed as it should. This section deals with that phase of the situation.
There is no use having an acquiescent president whose principal quality is his generous spirit and fairmindedness, unless you add to it a grim determination to carry through matters that may be entrusted to him for consideration.

speechtext: Judging from the hon. member's recent observations regarding the views of the leader of the opposition I should think it would be quite indifferent to him as to whether he heard or not. I mention that simply in passing.

speechtext: I did not say that, but if my right hon. friend wants it that way, I will leave it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I think the minister
should give consideration to this matter from the angles I suggest. I am now giving him the benefit of my not inconsiderable observations and experience in the matter. Of
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

course I would hesitate in a committee of the house to name a man, but the qualities required in an executive officer capable of discharging the duties which fall upon him are those not possessed by every man one meets. If you trust the operation of the system to an experienced railroad executive he must have knowledge of many things beyond the mere intricacies of the machine he is administering. For instance, the president of one of the great American railways is a Yale graduate whose knowledge of railroading might be less than that of a dozen men under him. But he has the qualities, vision, firmness and the ability to conceive and carry out plans of far-reaching consequence Therefore he is highly prized by the shareholders and directors. Perhaps the minister will recall that when Mr. Harriman consolidated his great roads, he took a lawyer from Texas and made him head of his system. The quality which makes a successful operating official is not the quality which makes him a successful executive. It will be recalled that the Canadian Pacific Railway was favoured with a rare combination in the presence on the board of directors of the late Sir William Van Home and the late Lord Shaughnessy. The two working together, one complementing the other, made a tremendous success of the administration of that property.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Were they college graduates?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I was not suggesting that they were graduates from anything other than the great school of experience and university of hard knocks. But since those days conditions have changed to a certain extent in connection with the administration of properties. I am not in any sense suggesting the desirability of or necessity for an appointee being a college graduate; that was not the point at all. My point was that in the realm of economics and theories we encounter conditions that are not of a practical kind, and if you entrust your fortunes ostensibly and openly to a skilled railway operator, and he commits his fortunes to the academic economist and theorist, you find yourself in a position not unlike that of the minister, himself, who found it desirable to eliminate from his speech certain sections that had been prepared for him by others who thought they knew more about the matter than he did. That is an apt illustration of what I desire to say. I have hesitated a great deal whether I should say as much as I have on this section. I have hesitated more as to whether I should not have said more because I realize perhaps to a greater degree than any other of this committee just what is involved in that section. I would like to see certain reforms effected, and I say to the minister frankly that they 
would have been effected along that very line whether he were in his present position or not. He will find that the same circumstances which developed, what some people call esprit de corps, in connection with the head office, but which those who know it more intimately would designate by another name, have led great railway corporations into taking most drastic action in England, the United States, and almost every country in the world, in dealing with their problems. That is the reason I have ventured to say what I have, believing the minister will recognize that I have done so only because of my deep conviction as to the necessity of there being concentrated effort, on the one hand, and firm and determined will, on the other, and a determination which will not be baulked by mere internal opposition or resistance. In giving effect to this section very great care will have to be exercised.
There is another section, Mr. Chairman, to which I might also refer without mentioning it by number, because it touches this only by way of argument. We talk of cooperation, and it will be remembered that we propose to continue cooperation between the two systems. No change has been made in that regard in this bill. We know now in the light of two years' experience the difficulties that have been encountered and the lack of really effective results.
It will be recalled that the report of the managers indicated a saving amounting to $1,000,000 in one year, which is a substantial sum of money, and a little less, I think, in another year. That is excellent, but we know, and the late government knew, the continued discussions, the continued negotiations, the continued meetings which were held, extending over weeks and months until finally the year came and went, and that was all. The minister must know by this time that for the last two years that has been going on, but there never was during all that time any suggestion that the arbitral tribunal should act. When I say suggestion, there may have been suggestions in discussion. I will put it in another way. There never was an appeal to the arbitral tribunal appointed under the act. Now the whole theory of the Duff report was that cooperation might bring a measure of success to both properties in which the country had a deep and abiding interest, owning the one and having a great stake in the other, not a financial stake in the same sense as it has in the Canadian National, but a national stake in the success of the other road. We know that these negotiations failed of result in the large sense that the Duff commission had in mind.

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
I put to the minister this: Does he think we ever can get anywhere with negotiations being carried on by representatives of the roads if in the midst of the meeting someone says: I must refer that to Ottawa? And then the minister becomes an absent negotiator, for he is not sitting at the table; he is having someone there representing his views. That was not the intention. The whole purpose was to try to create in this country as much as possible an independent body that would deal with another independent body subject to the restrictions imposed upon them by the statute. Responsibility must be accepted, and decisiveness must be evidenced by action. That has been the difficulty, and the minister knows that as well as I.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: That is not what Judge Fullerton says in his report. If I may be permitted, he said that the cooperating board of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway was composed of officials of the railways, and that they were more scared of competition than concerned with the public interest.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
But they were representatives of the railways, and the difficulty is that as representatives of the national railways, on the one hand they were thinking, as the hon. gentleman has said, in terms of fear of their competitors overreaching them, which is always a dangerous way of approach in negotiations, and, on the other they were wondering what the government thinks or will think of this. If one can get out of his mind that it is necessary to wonder what the government thinks or does not think, then one can begin to deal effectively in matters of administration, and can get results. That is the reason I make the suggestion. We had some experience two years ago, and one of the reasons I deprecate changes being made in this way is
that I had hoped there might be an improvement which would warrant the expectations that were entertained by the members of the Duff commission, and it is too bad in that sense that you have the termination of an arrangement which gave some hopeful signs of success. That is as far as I shall go. While those efforts have not been ended but are being continued under this legislation, the effect of this legislation is to leave them in an entirely different position from what they were under the former act, and my only suggestion to the minister is to make it clear to whoever is appointed under this section that there must be a sense of decisiveness, of reality and of finality that will make possible the attainment of results, instead of merely the continuation of negotiations over months reaching into years on matters which might have been quickly disposed of.
I shall give an illustration, and as it is a reflection upon the late government it cannot be said to be political. The representatives of the two companies met together and dealt with two problems, one express, and the other telegraphs, and they made recommendations. They had not concluded their final determination of the issues raised when they thought it desirable that legislation should be enacted of a permissive nature, only permissive, not representing an accomplished fact, but that would be available in the event of conclusions being reached. What happened? The government had courage enough to put the measure on the order paper, but that is as far as it ever went, and if the hon. gentleman seeks the reason all he needs to do, in the words on the monument to Sir Christopher Wren, is to look about him. He will look behind and in front, but however determined he may be he will not be able to carry his views into effect. In the essence, government is compromise; it is the surrender of your views to the views entertained by your colleagues. For instance, however strong my views may have been, those views could not prevail. It is idle to say that it is possible for the arbitrary will of any one man to be decisive with respect to matters over which he has no jurisdiction and which he must discuss with his colleagues and arrive at a middle course. The result was that the notice which appeared on the order paper never went any further. If the hon. gentleman is desirous of knowing how those who now sit about him felt about the matter, he will have no difficulty in ascertaining that. It was at once the subject of correspondence and public attacks and propaganda in the press in connection with loss of employment, whereas we were assured that that would not follow.
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

The matter was never completed, but I say to the minister that he will have to deal with it in the next few months. Therefore, it becomes of great importance that this section should be carried into effect in such a manner as will ensure the realization of the hopes of those who know, as I do, that in all these matters there is the personal equation which in the end determines to no inconsiderable extent the success or failure of your effort. You may have the highest minded industrialists in Canada sitting on your board, but in the end the success of this venture, as it is now provided for by this legislation, will depend upon the one or two or three entrusted with the power and authority to carry these views into effect. If the minister is to have in this venture the part that is contemplated by this legislation, I can only suggest to him the desirability of exercising the greatest care when the governor in council gives approval to some of the appointments that must be made.
I suggest to him, in all good will, that he will find that there has grown up in this corporation a situation not unlike that which has been known to exist in other great corporations. This is not unlike the so-called family compact, although it has nothing to do with family except as it is concerned with the law of self-preservation. I am suggesting to him what is known to every man who carefully observes and is willing to express an opinion. When the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) was discussing this matter-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
It is not necessary to say "hear, hear'"; that is quite apparent; it is "there, there," that I am thinking of. When the hon., member suggests that we are merely critical, I assure the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, that we have been something more than merely critical. I am grimly opposed-"grimly" is the right word-to the methods that have been adopted to accomplish the ends which the minister admits are aimed at. However, if we leave that out, the rest of the matter becomes a question of experience and observation, and of suggestion in the light of that experience and observation. He would be a very poor man indeed who had occupied any position in the public life of this country during the last four or five years, who could not make some suggestions that would be of value to those who have succeeded him. The suggestions might not be, and probably would not be, well received, but, on the other hand, the duty rests upon us to make suggestions, whether they are well received or not.

In all sincerity, and in the light of my own observations and experience, I say to the minister that there is a situation existing which I had made up my mind, and which I am sure he with his technical and professional experience will make up his mind, should be cured. This can be cured only in a manner that will be as ruthless as it will be efficient. When I say "ruthless," I mean that there must be no consideration of sentiment or of past services or of pleasing personalities; these factors must not stand in the way of the public interest. When I say "as ruthless as it will be efficient," I mean just what I say. When that power is exercised the efficiency will be increased many fold. I am not unmindful of the fact that the observations which I make will be misconstrued. That is not a matter of great importance to me because they are not difficult of understanding by those who wish to understand.
I do say-it has never been more apparent than just recently-that a condition exists which some would call intrigue, and which others would call something else. Stripped of everything, it is a combination of interests that aims to accomplish certain purposes. Despite what may be said, the fact is that the investigation which took place some years ago in the United States in connection with the transportation systems, and the investigation that took place in connection with the insurance companies, would make one realize how easy it is, even in this country, for efficiency to be restricted and lessened, not by conspiracy, far from it, but by those friendly understandings which are based upon a mutual desire to assist and are bottomed sometimes upon generous instincts of the human mind, which, nevertheless, in the end, operate very seriously against the success of the enterprise.
I say what I have to say on this section because I am greatly concerned with the whole situation. My experience and my observations lead me to make the remarks I have made. Possibly some members of the committee may think I should be more exact, but I prefer not to mention names. I leave it to the minister himself and to those who will be associated with him to ascertain just what reforms are necessary for the purpose of effecting the success of the operation of the undertaking in question.
