subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I wish to say just one word
in reply to the leader of the opposition. We must all remember one thing. He says that there has been a lack of cooperation between the two systems, as provided for in the act, but I would call his attention to this fact. In my own province we are struggling to live. In the old days the Dominion and Atlantic Railway was owned in England and was operated by Mr. Campbell and later by Mr. Gifkins. One day it became the property of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. First, they had it declared to be a road for the general advantage of Canada and then they purchased it, or at least they secured a majority of the common stock, which gave them control. They came down and rented at a high rate to the Dominion and Atlantic Railway cars that were as old-fashioned as the chariots in which Caesar rode in Rome. Canadian Pacific officials came down later on, when these cars were still there, took off the letters "D.A.R." and substituted "C.P.R.," and they ripped off the "D.A.R." buttons from the coats of the officials and put on "C.P.R." buttons. They also changed the stationery. That was the first evidence of good will to the people of Nova Scotia. I am not complaining particularly of that, but what happened? It was the beginning of a movement to destroy the esprit de corps of which the leader of the opposition has spoken this afternoon. To
make matters worse they removed the auditing branch from Nova Scotia to Montreal, throwing people out of work in our province.
No more, there is no more
To live for now.
My king is false,
My hope betrayed;
My father, O! the worth,
The gloriousness and the loveliness
Has passed away from earth.
Then they issued an order that all car repairs were to be made in Montreal, the engines to be taken out of Nova Scotia to that city for overhauling, so that by degrees they closed the machine shops in Nova Scotia, there being but a limited number of men there to-day. But did they stop there? No. There is a rumour, which I believe to be true, that the general manager of the line is to be retired on pension and that the operation of that railway is to be from Montreal and not in Nova Scotia. By degrees they have sucked the very lifeblood of that little line in my province in order to bolster up their assets, taking the property of the "D.A.R.", as it is called, and making it a part of the Canadian Pacific Railway so as to make a favourable annual statement. Not only that; I believe it is the intention to have merely a sort of superintendent and to have the "D.A.R." go through that lovely land of Evangeline from Halifax to Yarmouth. We are inviting tourists to our province though the hearts of our people are heavy, for these people have been thrown out of employment in order that the work they were doing should now be carried on in Montreal. In this respect the little province of Nova Scotia, the province next to New Brunswick in which my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition was born, is being discriminated against. Can we have any prosperity under these conditions, far removed as we are from the centre of things, with a high tariff wall against us in the United States, though it '.s true that wall has been somewhat lowered? With proper transportation facilities we might have gone into the New England market, but we have been cut off by a high tariff wall, and the general freight structure has operated against us, with the result that our industrial activities have been dwindling. It is fortunate that we have had some men- perhaps I may be pardoned if I say that I am one of them-who have been instrumental in saving one or two industries in the province, including the Acadia Sugar Refinery, which gives employment to some 400 people. In all, about 2,500 people would have been
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

seriously affected if the rates had not been fixed so as to permit this industry to operate.
Sir Edward Beatty may be a graduate of McGill; he may be a man of high social standing; he may be the essence and indeed the quintessence of higher society in this country. But I want to say to my right hon. friend that if that ruthlessness to which he has referred is to be applied in the same way to the man who takes his cocktail in the club as to the man who wears overalls, then it is all right. Otherwise it is wrong, and the people of Canada will ever remember the statement the right hon. gentleman made in the house this afternoon in that regard. Sir Edward Beatty sent down the late Mr. Grant Hall, the vice-president, to a meeting of the Eastern Steamship company, putting Canadian money into an American concern. The steamers Prince Arthur, Prince George and Prince Edward, built by the Dominion and Atlantic Railway, had proved satisfactory on the route between Yarmouth and Boston, but what did Sir Edward Beatty do? He entered into an arrangement with this American concern, the Eastern Steamship company, with the result that on that trade route on which ships flying the British flag had operated, and on which Nova Scotians had been engaged, from captains down to sailors, the Eastern Steamship company took over the business at the instance of Sir Edward Beatty and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

The leader of the opposition dealt with the question of cooperation, urging that in order to secure the necessary esprit de corps and fairness, even ruthless methods should be resorted to. Surely if he could elaborate on that I have a right to point out that the very essence of that cooperation is lacking as between that part of our transportation system owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the part owned by the people. I am arguing that the rights and privileges of the people of Nova Scotia in this connection should not be handed over to the people to the south of us. I am sure that, upon reflection, the chairman will realize that I do not desire to transgress the rules. Although I will bow to his ruling, I do not believe I am without the rule; I believe I am within it. Perhaps I may be permitted to continue hewing close

to the line, in the direction I am going. I shall be through in five minutes, and there will be no more "Order," and, I hope, no more disorder.

speechtext: I did not hear all the remarks of the hon. member for Halifax, but I did hear him say that he would finish in five minutes, and if so, I am quite in accord.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, it will take me only five minutes; when I return to that little province by the sea it will be known that I have been permitted to go on if I shall confine my remarks to five minutes, and they will see the hard-heartedness of this chairman and his strict administration and interpretation of the rules as applied to one of the members for Halifax as against the right hon. leader of the opposition. My only object in desiring to be heard is that some benefits may come to the people of a province that I love, as I love also the rest of Canada, and want to see all the dominion develop equally, so that we shall not lag so far behind. It was in reference to that I was speaking of the Yarmouth Steamship Company, started by a Nova Scotian, L. E. Baker, who put everything he had into it, desiring its development and prosperity, and who died practically without anything. Then came the Dominion Atlantic Railway Steamship Company, then the Canadian Pacific Railway control and management; then followed the disappearance of the Dominion Atlantic Railway Steamship Company and the arrival of the Eastern Steampship company's boats, the Evangeline, the Yarmouth, the Acadia, and the Saint John, four boats, with a bonus of forty per cent by the American government, a sixty per cent loan on which they have not paid interest, and a subsidy of $500,000 for carrying the mails in the winter across the Bay of Fundy.
The word from Washington under the late President Hoover was that the coastal trade of the United States must be built up, and they built it up with the resources of 130 millions of people. Our relationships with the people of that country are splendid, but if

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
things are to be done in that way we in the province of Nova Scotia might as well know it, and the sooner the message of sudden death is pronounced the more quickly we shall realize our position. The statements I make cannot be controverted. To-day the Eastern Steamship company, at the solicitation of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who are owners of stock in the American company, are running between Boston and Yarmouth. What has been the result? Our captains, chief officers and second officers, born in Nova Scotia, took up residence in Boston, became American citizens, took their examinations, became masters and mates under the American flag, and returned on the bridge and on the deck of those ships to Yarmouth, leaving Yarmouth as Nova Scotians and coming back as aliens. Is this the evidence of the policy of cooperation of which the leader of the opposition speaks? I bring this to his attention. Are Sir Edward Beatty, the Canadian Pacific Railway and its management, the brains behind this? The right hon. gentleman differentiates between Lord Shaughnessy and Sir William Van Home, and Mr. Beatty because times are different. Times may change, but hearts and minds do not, and I state to my right hon. friend that, while I want to see this road a success, I desire also to see placed in charge men who have hearts as well as minds, and that the man who wears the overalls shall not be ruthlessly removed while those in the higher-up sections of their company are continued in office. How is it possible for us in Nova Scotia to have faith in Sir Edward Beatty and his management? I should like to ask the right hon. leader of the opposition the question: Is he in agreement with Sir Edward Beatty in the handing over of that trade route between Yarmouth and Boston to the Eastern Steamship company and the American flag and making Americans of Nova Scotians? Is he in favour of that or is he not? I await his answer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: As we deal with that I have only this to say. To provide that a mere four of seven directors can sign a minute, without any provision that it shall be incorporated in the minutes of the corporation, is unsound. The original section in the old act was not as full as it should have been; I saw that when, unfortunately, it was too late. There should be a provision that a minute which is unanimously agreed upon, as evidenced1 by the writing of all the members who are expressing their acquiescence, should be incorporated in the minute book of the corporation. That is a matter which experience has shown to be highly desirable. I think the section should be amended in that regard. The minister can speak to the leader of the senate with respect to the matter. To leave it as it is now is rather a dangerous procedure. There is nothing, as the minister sees, that contemplates a minute thus arrived at finding its place in the minute book of the corporation, and with his experience of companies he knows, perhaps, that the court of appeal in England decided many years ago that although a director might be in the room and two others just outside, and a quorum present, they were not present unless they were in the same room. This is in derogation of the common law provision; it provides that a minute signed by all shall have the same force and effect as though it were passed at a meeting, but there is nothing to provide that it shall be entered in the minute book as part of the proceedings of the corporation. Perhaps this paragraph might stand and the minister can speak to his leader in the senate who has the bill in charge there. I have no desire to hold up this paragraph, but certainly as it stands now it is not very satisfactory.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: This has to do with the budget, and I have before me a notation as to a suggestion I should like to make. I assume that the minister is anxious to get this bill to the other house, but this paragraph .provides that the budget shall be submitted to the Minister of Transport, while the next paragraph provides that the annual report shall be submitted to parliament also through the Minister of Transport. The minister will perhaps recall that as the law now stands the budget has to be submitted to the Minister of Finance, and with all deference I suggest to the minister who is in charge of the bill that the Minister of Finance is the person to whom the budget should go, for he is responsible for finding the money. There was some discussion about this matter when the other bill was under consideration, and the general view was that the Minister of Finance as distinguished from the Minister of Railways should receive the budget for the purpose of submitting it to his colleagues in council. He must consider it first of all from the standpoint of his ability to raise the money required by the railway company. I do not know whether or not there is any reason behind this change, but I suggest that it would be better to retain the supremacy of the Minister of Finance over the budget as it reaches council. It is only a question of how it shall reach council, whether through the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Transport, but I submit that the Minister of Finance would be the proper person. That is what we have in the old act, and perhaps this change was made inadvertently. I do not think it serves any useful purpose.

The board of directors or a majority thereof may without meeting decide or act by way of a written minute or concurrence signed by the directors or a majority of them and entered in the minute book of the board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL

speechtext: I shall be glad to look into the matter. It is practically six o'clock now, and I am afraid we shall hardly finish this bill by that time, so after dinner I shall bring in an amendment to that paragraph.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: May I point out what I have just said to my colleague. I think it highly undesirable that a minute of that kind, signed by a majority and never communicated bo the minority, should have the force of a binding minute, because the other three members might never have heard of it. In practice my view has been that a minute signed by all the directors should have the force of a minute passed by the majority and entered in the minute book. If the minute is signed by all of them-one might be in Saskatoon, another in Halifax and a third somewhere else; sometimes you telegraph the substance of the minute to them and they telegraph their consent before it is signed-it should have the force of a minute, but as the paragraph reads, it is provided that a majority may sign that minute and give it the power and authority of a minute passed at a meeting held by the directors where the pros and cons could be considered. As the paragraph now reads, only four need sign and the other three might know nothing about the minute. They might have great opposition to it, such opposition as might prevent its being passed if the meeting were held. That is the point I was endeavouring to make.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
On this clause I should like to move an addition. Yesterday I indicated that I would move an amendment to clause 4 in connection with the pay of employees dismissed from the service as a result of cooperation between the two railways. At that time the suggestion was made that this was the proper point at which to move the amendment. I made the statement yesterday that in 1933 the main purpose behind the measure was to provide a certain amount of cooperation between the two railways, and I stated that this bill is a further step in the same direction. When the minister spoke upon introducing the amendments to the 1933 legislation he claimed that one of the reasons for the changes set out in the present bill was that there were not sufficient cooperative measures instituted between the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. When I made that statement yesterday the minister said that I had misquoted him, and as a result of his observations I withdrew my statement. These are the words I used:
The act of 1933 was an act to provide for looperation between the two railways, and if I remember aright-and I hope the minister will tell me if I am wrong-when he introduced the present bill he said that one of the reasons for the changes proposed was that there had not been sufficient cooperation between the two railways.
Mr. Howe: The hon. member asked me to correct him if he were wrong, and I shall be glad to do so. I said nothing of the kind.
Mr. Heaps: Then I apologize to the minister.
Then I did apologize. May I proceed to quote what the Minister of Railways said. Upon introducing the bill on April 27, he is reported at page 2178 of Hansard as follows:
To date they have failed to achieve any substantial cooperative economies, to secure which was the principal object of their appointment and the outstanding feature of the 1933 legislation. Not only have they failed to
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

secure any substantial results to date, but on their own published statements, the prospect of future results from cooperative measures, plans and arrangements is not bright.
Then, as reported on the following page, he made this statement:
Two annual reports from the Canadian National trustees, but one continuous recitation of apologies for lack of success in applying the cooperative provisions of the 1933 act under which they were appointed.
I take it that in itself is sufficient indication of the purposes underlying the introduction of the present measure. While I withdrew any statement I made with regard to the minister, after he denied having made such observations, I somehow feel that my withdrawal of the statement I made in committee yesterday was not entirely warranted.
I made the claim yesterday that employees of the railways find themselves in a different position from that enjoyed by men working for private companies, when such companies voluntarily arrange to amalgamate and thereby save expenses by way of reduction in either labour or overhead. In the present instance we have a government owned utility. We have another utility which is under government regulation. Now we bring in legislation compelling the two railway companies to do certain things. One thing we compel them to do is to cooperate their services and thereby bring about certain economies in costs of operation. It has been stated often that the large amount of economies to be effected as a result of cooperation of the services will be at the expense of those who are employed on the railways. In other words, the working men will be the main sufferers as a result of the legislation. May I quote what Mr. Justice Fullerton said to the committee on Tuesday:
Perhaps the greatest difficulty in the way of expediting further extensive economies concerns labour. To reduce expenses on any large scale men must be displaced, and if serious hardship and unrest are to be avoided, some form of dismissal pay or compensation should be considered. It is my personal view that a great deal more progress might be made in cooperative measures for economy, as well as in other economy measures, if some plan for employee dismissal compensation were worked out, and adopted. I believe it to be a fact that the officials of the railroad, contemplating changes designed to secure economy but which involve putting men out of work with little hope of reemployment,-
I want that to be borne in mind by the members of this committee, that there is little hope of reemployment.
-are influenced by humanitarian feelings, and naturally the men resist all such measures to the limit. It does not seem unreasonable to urge that part of the advantage to the

employers should be shared with labour, rather than that the whole burden should be borne by labour. The Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act requires that both the burden and the advantage should be shared by the two companies. It seems to have been overlooked that the joint advantage can be secured only by transferring the burden to labour. A more equitable arrangement with labour appear to be required and should be provided. If this were done, one great preliminary step towards the accomplishment of any radical changes which might displace labour would be made.
A little further down, on the same page, Mr. Justice Fullerton said:
Nevertheless, I am convinced that the greatest obstacle to cooperative measures is consideration for the men who would be displaced by their adoption. An agreement has been reached between the railway executives and organized labour in the United States providing for the payment of a measure of compensation to employees thrown out of work by consolidation of railway facilities, and I understand that the British railways also made some provision for employes displaced as a result of the amalgamation of British railways into four systems.
I have reached the conclusion that the government, the railways, and the representatives of railway labour-
May I point out to the minister that Mr. Justice Fullerton, chairman of the board of trustees, places a responsibility here upon the government as well as upon the railway companies.
-should discuss this matter together with a view to the adoption of some arrangement for the two Canadian railroads as will afford reasonable protection against hardship on the part of these employees who, after long years of service, may be displaced by the adoption of cooperative methods.
May I point out the anomalous position in which the railways of this country and their employees might find themselves? Both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway have large interests in the United States. The Canadian National Railways own quite a valuable piece of railway, I understand, between Detroit and Chicago, and they have also large interests in the Central Vermont railway, which was referred to this afternoon by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). The Canadian Pacific Railway have also interests in railway lines in the United States. Yet, Mr. Chairman, the employees in the United States of these two railways, if cooperative measures are adopted there, will become the beneficiaries of certain agreements arrived at with the railway companies while the employees in this country of these two roads will not be eligible for the same benefits. I think that is most unfair. I noticed the other day when the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. JUNE 5, 1936
CJVJ2.-Board oj Directors
Mackenzie King) introduced a measure for the amalgamation of various departments, he stated that there would be no dismissals of employees in the various services of the government; in other words, the employees were to be protected. I am simply asking this committee to give in this legislation the same consideration to the employees of both the government owned road and the privately owned road. I think that is not an unfair request to make. In the United States the railway companies and their employees have arrived at a basis of understanding by which dismissal pay is going to be given to the men who will be displaced as a result of the amalgamation of services. Why cannot we do the same thing in this country? If the government are not willing to introduce legislation along that line, at least let them take the same stand that has been taken in the United States.
I do not have to go into the whole question why men are entitled to compensation upon being dismissed after long years of service on behalf of the railways because that question has been gone into in years gone by, and even during this session it has been spoken to by many members on both sides of the house. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am going to move that the following be added to section 4 on page 8 of Bill No. 21 now before us:
An employee of the railway companies affected by this act who as a result of cooper- . ation of services between the railways loses his or her employment shall be entitled to compensation, and the amount of such compensation shall be determined by a board of three to be appointed, one by the employees, one by the railways, and a third who shall be chairman of the board to be selected by the two representatives already appointed.
In the event of failure to select a third member of the board, such appointment shall be made by the Minister of Labour.
The funds for such compensation awards and expenses in connection therewith shall be derived from a levy on the gross receipts of the two railways, and the award of the board shall in all cases be final.
I know that I may be met with some difficulties from the Chair. I anticipate that, for I remember that when I moved an almost identical motion in 1933, different only in phraseology, the point was raised that the amendment was out of order, and the Chair ruled my motion out of order on grounds that I could not understand. I was extremely honoured, however, 'to have on my side at that time members of the Liberal party who were then in the house, supporting my contention that the motion was perfectly in order. I hope they will be just as anxious to support 12739-220
this present motion of mine as they were in 1933. I know they do not sit on the same side of the house now, and a great deal depends upon which side of the Speaker one sits as to the viewpoint one will take on particular questions. But the point I want to emphasize in arguing that this amendment is perfectly in order is the fact that its final clause provides that:
The funds for such compensation awards and expenses in connection therewith shall be derived from a levy on the gross receipts of the two railways, and the award of the board shall in all cases be final.
In other words, it is a fund which is to be created by the two railways themselves, and is not money which is voted by parliament out of taxation raised in the dominion. Under those circumstances I think the amendment is perfectly in order. But, assuming for the sake of argument that a private member is not allowed to move such an amendment, and I have a very strong suspicion, Mr. Chairman, which way your riding is going to be-

In a general way that
meets with the views which I suggested to the committee just before we rose at six o'clock, although I would have used a little different language. But that is not a matter of importance as I think the idea is adequately expressed. The point is this-and I think the minister will at once realize the effect of it

that a unanimous minute signed by all without discussion or meeting shall be regarded as the equivalent of a majority decision after discussion at a meeting of the board. I think that is a salutary and sound! rule in view of the decisions that there is no valid meeting of the board called to consider a subject matter unless the members are present in the room. That is, you cannot have one member in one room, another in another room and then say that they were both present and that a decision was arrived at after discussion. Unanimity would seem to be desirable, but that was not the purpose the minister had in mind in drafting the amendment. He contemplates the possibility of a majority decision and it seems to me that he has safeguarded the matter by saying that notice of the subject matter shall be given to all directors. If one or two directors telegraphed and said that they were opposed to a certain matter, it is not probable that the other directors would sign a minute unless there was a formal meeting with discussion.

I should like to point out that practically the same amendment was moved by the hon. member
[The Chairman.]
on April 7, 1933. At that time a point of order was raised by the then Minister of Railways, Mr. Manion. I spoke on the point of order as follows:
Speaking to the point of order, as this bill removes entirely from parliament the control of the expenditures of the Canadian National Railways, I do not think the point of order is well taken, because the levy proposed is upon an industry which by the terms of this legislation is no longer within the purview of the minister or of parliament. If it were otherwise, the point of order raised by the minister would be well taken.
I submit that under the legislation now before the committee, all the revenues of the Canadian National Railways will be under the control of the minister and of parliament, and therefore the point of order raised on April 7, 1933, by the former Minister of Railways and Canals would be quite valid with reference to this amendment. The hon. member moved a further amendment on May 9 of that year, and another amendment was moved on May 9 by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth). The latter amendment was ruled out of order by the Speaker. The hon. member's amendment read:
That the said bill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that the following clause be inserted:
"That the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railway Company shall provide compensation to those whose services will be dispensed with as a result of the operation of any of the provisions of this act."
This amendment was ruled out of order, which ruling was sustained on division. On three separate occasions during the debate of 1933 the same point of order was raised and was sustained each time by the house. While I do not believe that the fears of my hon. friend have any justification, he knows as well as I do that it is not within the purview of a private member to move such an amendment.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order. I think the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) is stretching the point considerably when he ventures to say that under this proposed set-up all the expenditures of the Canadian National Railways will be under the control of this parliament. As a matter of fact, I do not think anyone could argue that seriously. It is quite true that under this legislation there will be a little more immediate responsibility to parliament, but the railway will still have a large measure of discretion in regard to its expenditures. The proposed amendment is that such compensation awards and expenses

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
in connection therewith shall be derived from a levy on the gross receipts of the two railways, and the award of the board shall in all cases be final. That cannot, by any stretch of the imagination, be called taxation. In the strict sense of the word, the gross receipts of the railways are not government moneys. There is not any added expenditure proposed, and it is not in any sense taxation. Hence, I do not think the minister can say that the situation is radically different from what it was when we proposed this amend-mfent in 1933. As a matter of fact, I think that whatever change there is comes largely because of the changed position of the minister, who now is sitting to the right of the Speaker instead of to the left.

speechtext: If I may speak on the point of order, the whole question is as to whether this involves taxation or expenditures from the supply granted to His Majesty. This amendment asks that the revenues of the two railways, derived from the various services which they render to the public of this country, shall be utilized to provide a fund out of which compensation shall be paid to the employees of the roads. I do not think it can be argued that the question of taxation enters into the matter. The point might be stretched to the extent of saying that the government might have to pay the deficit of the Canadian National Railways, and there might be something in the argument if it were said that the government was to be directly responsible for such compensation awards. But we are not asking the government to be responsible; we are asking that the railways themselves be responsible by a levy on their gross receipts to provide a fund from which the men affected may receive compensation. For that reason I believe the amendment is perfectly in order.

In Canada we have the most advanced laws with respect to railway labour of any country on

the north American continent, this being the only country which has a complete pension system for employees. That was not the result of legislation but was worked out by mutual arrangement between the railways and their employees. The United States government a year ago adopted a compulsory pension scheme for railway employees, but it has not been made operative. On most of the railways in the United States we find that there is no pension scheme or, if there is, it is only on a small scale, not on the scale that we have in Canada. speechtext:
It is the easiest thing in the world for hon. members to shout "order." Anyone can do that; it does not require brains to do that. As a rule I do not stray very far from the proper procedure. I try to conduct myself with decorum.and in keeping with the rules of the house and I do not attempt to shout anyone down. I have enough confidence in the Chair to adhere 'to the proper .procedure. I thought, however, that when the Minister of Railways had referred, not altogether in any complimentary way, to the resolution I had proposed, the least I could do was to say a word in reply. The minister has expressed sympathy with the men who may be affected by the provisions of this clause. A good deal of sympathy has been expressed in various quarters in that connection, and the minister cited what has been done in the United States. I think it is a fact, however, that what happened in the United States was due to legislation which was pending. I hold that had no legislation been pending in the United States there would have been no agreement with respect to paying anything to the men who were dismissed as a result of the amalgamation of services there. I do not think the minister would care to deny that statement. It was because legislation was pending, because the president of the United States had himself taken an interest in the matter and was convinced that something should be done for the railway men so affected, that the employers took action and reached an agreement with the men. The minister is not less sympathetic than officials in the United States, and there is a great deal of sympathy all round for the men in this country. But I submit that unless this parliament takes concrete action, all the sympathy in the world will be of little avail so far as the men themselves are concerned. All I plead for this evening is that consideration be given these men, who have a right to expect protection from this committee. They have a right to expect protection from this committee and they are not receiving it. All the minister says is that we should not interfere between the railway companies and the men. We are not interfering, in the sense that is implied, between the railway companies and the men. But may I point out that every piece of legislation we put on the statute books of this country is interference with somebody, in some way, shape or form. I know what this legislation involves. Through it we are threatening the livelihood of many thousands of railway employees in the dominion, and we are making no provision for the men so affected. The

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
government tell us that by this legislation they are going to solve in some degree our unemployment problem. I venture to say that by this legislation they are going to aggravate the existing unemployment problem without making provision for those affected, and all I suggest to the government, the minister and those associated with him is that they take some definite action so that the men who may be thus affected will be properly and adequately protected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I speak to the point out of some experience as a former Minister of Railways, not for the purpose of creating dissension, but out of some knowledge of the complicated structure of agreements which exist between recognized representatives of railway men in this country and the two great railway corporations. There is no better organized class of men in Canada than our railway employees, and I think I can say that no trades union organizations are better led than those representing our transportation employees. By this action of my hon. friends, which admittedly is not at the request of the men's organizations, nor at the request of the two great employers of railway labour in this country, the idea is that, in spite of the relations existing to which I have referred, this parliament should come along with some arbitrary method whereby an adjustment between the railways and their employees shall take place. From experience I can say that in the past the railway unions always asked me as Minister of Railways to leave them free to negotiate with the management of the railroad with respect to any matter affecting the welfare of the employees. That is the basic principle upon which the organizations have operated for many years, and in the main, I believe, successfully. There is no doubt at all that this problem must be faced. There is no opposition to the idea, which my hon. friend seeks to convey, from the employers, as was I believe the case in the United States. In this country, instead of having a great number of railway companies we have just the two great railway corporations and a few smaller ones which in practice always follow along in connection with agreements between employer and employee. The heads of both these two great systems recognize in principle that this problem must be met and must be negotiated to a satisfactory conclusion. That being the case, I submit, with all deference to my hon. friend, who I know speaks in a political capacity for labour, that on this occasion he is not speaking for the organized bodies directly interested in the matter. If he is, I am very much surprised, because it represents a completely new departure by the organized workers in the railway service for them to take an action at this time without having first approached their employers through the medium of their own organizations, under the terms of their own agreements, and endeavoured to work out a solution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I did not say that. I wish the hon. member would try to keep within reason on this matter. He objects to being called to order, but he never sticks to a point, as far as I have been able to hear, and I have listened to him carefully since I have been in this house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
There is no point of order in that, of course, but I think hon. gentlemen will hardly say that I do not stick to my point. My understanding of the minister's words is as I have given it. If the minister undertakes to give another meaning to those words I hope he will tell us very clearly their real meaning and the real purpose of bringing in this bill.
Now I should like to refer to another statement made by the minister. He says that this matter could be best arranged by some agreement which he thinks might be made quite independently of legislation. Let me point out that in this country the Canadian National is a national system. A few minutes ago, thotigh in one sense we represent the shareholders of the system, we were not permitted to pass regulations with regard to these railways because they came directly under the government. The government have thought it desirable to introduce pension schemes in connection with the civil service. If the argument advanced by the minister has any validity at all, the railway employees are coming very close to the point where they will be directly under government control, and in that case surely there cannot be any very great objection to this government instituting something analogous to provisions it makes for its own employees.
Now I come to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), I think it was, that even though the Chair has ruled that we cannot introduce a motion providing for compensation, it would be quite proper for the government to give serious consideration to bringing in an arrangement by which compensation might be given railway employees for loss of work caused by legislation of this kind. Last night when we were on section 2 I was prevented from reading the arrangements that are now in effect in the United States. Perhaps I might now be given an opportunity to read two or three paragraphs summarizing those arrangements. I quote from Labour of May 26:
No employee's wages will be reduced if, as the result of a consolidation, he is placed on a job paying a lower rate.
Displaced employees will be paid coordination allowances ranging from sixty per cent of their wages for five years for men in the

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
fifteen year service fist down to a "grub stake" of two months' full wages for men with less than twelve months' service. These men will hold reemployment, free transportation, hospitalization and other rights.
At the option of the employee, a cash lump sum settlement may be paid to him and he gives up all rights to reemployment, etc. Under this plan men with five to fifteen years' service can get immediate cash equal to one year's full pay.
In the three to five year service group the cash allowance is nine months' pay. Two to three year men can get six months' pay in cash. Those in the one to two year class get six months' wages if they take the dismissal allowance instead of coordination benefits. If the men with less than one year's service want immediate cash they can get it on the basis of five days' pay for each month they have worked.
Moving expenses and property losses of transferred employees will be paid.
Railroads which are parties to the agreement agree not to coordinate with any carrier which has not signed the agreement until the latter provides the same protection guaranteed by the signatory roads.
I have read an outline of the agreement recently brought into existence in the United States. It seems to me that some similar provision and some method acceptable to the government ought to be introduced to safeguard the rights of our Canadian railway workers. Let me point out that if workers on the Canadian National Railways went on strike there would be an immediate outcry across Canada that those men were operating a government railway. I would be one of the first to protest against that interpretation of their position, but there is no doubt that there would be a great outcry to the effect that those men are in a position of responsibility. The statement would be made that they are operating a government railway and ought not to go on strike. Any really effective movement of that kind which might be made in an attempt to force the hands of the employers would immediately bring down the condemnation of the government; I have no doubt of that.
We are attempting to adopt a method by which the rights of the men may be safeguarded peaceably and without any dislocation. I should like to say, however, that when we introduced a similar amendment three years ago, the Minister of Railways and Canals in the late administration suggested that it would be a good thing to do this a little later on, when any employees were adversely affected. These last three years have demonstrated that many employees have been adversely affected. I said upon that occasion that I thought the time to introduce measures of this kind was at the time legislation was being set up, and I still think so. We now take this opportunity to place this

proposal before the government, in the hope that it may be included in the bill.
In closing, may I say that while I cannot argue against economies of any kind, from what I have read I am firmly convinced that the economies contemplated are nothing like as great as they are made out to be. Mr. Beatty himself has been unable to point to just where the great economies may be secured. In my view the pleas for economy have not been sustained by the facts. If we are going to put the whole transportation system under the government, I, with a socialist viewpoint, would say that might be a proper procedure, although I should hate to have the whole system placed under the present government. But under a socialist regime we might very well have coordination of all transportation and communication facilities. I say, however, that under present circumstances we in the labour movement are opposed to chiselling in, in such a way that under the name of "cooperation" we get a very large measure of amalgamation. Any economies are being made at the expense of the employee for the sake of the bondholders; that is the trouble.
What have we in the way of cooperation today? Yesterday in the Quebec legislature a bill was passed by which the Canadian Pacific Railway will go into a territory which all along has been supposed to be that of the Canadian National Railways. Is that cooperation? Now we have a bill introduced in this house the effect of which will be to send a branch line of the Canadian National Railways into that territory. That is not cooperation. If the Canadian Pacific Railway wanted to take action along the lines of the legislation secured in the provincial legislature they ought first to have gone to the board of railway commissioners and inquired about the situation. They should have come to this parliament and submitted their bill. We cannot have cooperation which simply means that employees are ground down and dismissed to effect economies, when at the same time, if they take the notion, the railways may spend tens of millions of dollars to carry through undertakings completely out of harmony with the spirit of cooperation. These are matters which must be considered.
Hence I would urge upon the minister that the new board should not be instructed in any way to foster cooperation of the kind we have had in the past. If the new board is to be more directly amenable to the government, the government which to a great extent won its majority in railway districts on the understanding that the Liberal party was opposed to amalgamation, that govern-

C.N.It.-Board of Directors
ment I would hope would instruct the new board of directors and the new management to halt the progress of "cooperation," in so far as it is more or less a disguised step towards amalgamation.

Mr. TAY'LOR (Nanaimo): Thank you very much, but you realize the implications attaching to the decision of the chairman.

speechtext:
It strikes me that there is involved in the question of compensa tion something which has so far been a hindrance to the carrying out of the principle of cooperation. That seems to be evident from the statement of the chairman of the board of trustees and also from the statement of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) as it is published in the proceedings of the committee.
I think perhaps the best friends of the railway organizations would be well advised if they accepted the word of the government and the suggestion of the minister of transport that in the matter of cooperation provision would be made for compensation. I believe it would lot be wise to have that provision made in this bill. Nevertheless, in view of the fact that the chairman of the board of trustees made it perfectly clear that one hindrance to further cooperation was the fact that the burden of it would of necessity have been transferred to labour, the whole situation becomes important when we consider any further

cooperation between the two great systems. I do not believe that the directors will succeed in further cooperation unless the board feels itself able to meet the question of compensation with a reasonably free hand. The president of the Canadian Pacific Railway has on more than one occasion, according to reports in the press, made it clear that he did not want cooperation if it meant employees of the railway losing their positions. That statement has been made by advocates of cooperation in this house during this session of parliament, and it is tacitly made by the present minister in his reply before the railway committee to the chairman of the board of trustees. It seems to me that there should be a fairly definite understanding in order that the men in the employ of both companies may feel assured that the process of cooperation, however far it may go, will not have the effect of placing their positions or their earnings in jeopardy.
Of course, as I understand this whole problem, there is a far greater scope for the management of both roads, particularly the management of the public road, in broadening out its sphere of activities, enlarging the scope of action of the board of directors, reaching out for new business and bringing in a return which will, in the words of the minister, ultimately wipe out the huge deficit we have to face each year. If we succeed in doing that, that is the real purpose of the legislation before this committee, not ascribing motives such as have been mentioned during the discussion this afternoon, yesterday and on other occasions when this matter has been before us. I hope to see this legislation bear fruit such as the minister of transport has suggested it is likely to do, and I believe it will if all parties in this chamber forget the ascribing of unworthy motives to one another, unite, with the common purpose of trying to salvage what may be salvaged from this splendid asset and give this dominion an up to date system of transportation which will meet the needs of the various portions of this dominion, and meet particularly the needs of industry, which I am satisfied it is not doing at the present time.
