speechtext: With the consent of the house, I should like to move the third reading now as we are anxious to get this bill to the other chamber.
Motion agreed to, and bill read the third time and passed.
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Fruit, including grant of $4,750 to Canadian Horticultural Council, $460,200.
Will the minister explain the decrease in this vote?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):

speechtext: What is the increase for?

The original grant of $5,000 was reduced by ten per cent, and the reduction this year is only five per cent. Unforeseen expenses: 1935-36, $254.50; 1936-37, $118, a decrease of $136.50. When the decreases and increases are totalled up, it will be found that the total decrease is $15,660.48.
The minister mentioned an amount of something like $3,500 for advertising. Is this the total amount expended to advertise Canada's fruit crops?
That item is for publications and bulletins. It is not advertising; it is largely information furnished to people who are growing fruit.
Is there any amount under any other heading for advertising the fruit production of Canada?
There is nothing provided at the moment for that purpose.
The minister mentioned an amount of $225,407 for outside salaries. Would that be for inspectors?
That is mostly for inspection services throughout the country.
Would that include experimental farms?
No; it has nothing to do with the experimental farms. This is inspection work throughout the country in connection with fruit growing, fruit grading and the general administration of the fruit act.
What is the difference in the grants this year and last year to the seed fairs?
That would come under the next item.
I understood that the item had been passed. Was the grant last year the same?
There is a slight decrease I gave all the particulars. It is $15,660.48 less on the total vote.

Item agreed to.
Supply-Agriculture
Seed, feed and fertilizer control, including grants to seed fairs, et cetera, also grant of $18,900 to Canadian Seed Growers' Association, $407,200.

On February 28 we
covered this entire vote and all explanations were given. Eleven o'clock came before the item could carry. The information will be found in Hansard of that day.
Does this include the funds required for freight charges on seed grain shipped to farmers from seed cleaning establishments ?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Entomology, including investigations and inspections relating to destructive insects and pests, $400,100.
This item was called earlier in the session, but the leader of the opposition asked to have it stand because some members were not present.
What work is carried on at Indian Head with regard to cutworms and grasshoppers?

The entomological work is not done at experimental farms. There are two different branches, the experimental farm branch and this particular branch. A certain amount of research work is done in connection with insects and other pests at different experimental farms throughout the country. One of the pests in the west is the cutworm and another is the wheat stem sawfly. Most of the work done at the entomological laboratory at Indian Head is in connection with pests of that kind, and information is given the farmers from time to time as to how to deal with them.

Can the minister give us information with regard to cooperation with the provinces? The act with regard to insects and pests is under the administration of the dominion government, but in connection with certain work-for instance in the fire blight experiments, though I am not quite sure whether that comes under this item-operations are carried on by both the province and the dominion, in British Columbia and possibly in other provinces.

There is cooperation between the provinces and the dominion. It will be understood, of course, that when an insect of any kind attacks, say spruce trees or any other forest trees, it does not stop its operations at provincial boundaries but extends from one province into another. This is true of grasshoppers and other insect pests. It is necessary, therefore, to have the greater

part of the work done by the dominion. The provinces cooperate to the fullest extent whenever any pest is being attacked. We have the fullest cooperation from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Quebec in fighting certain pests in the east; we have cooperation in British Columbia, and we have cooperation in the prairie provinces in connection with insects that attack the grain crops.
Was this cooperation a matter particularly under discussion at the dominion-provincial conference?

Yes; it was discussed in a general way though there was no detailed discussion. The question of overlapping was discussed and it was decided that there had been the fullest cooperation in this regard.
Does the department contemplate any action in connection with the wireworm, in the way of cooperation with the provincial departments?
An experiment is being carried on at Swift Current for the purpose of providing the best information available with regard to attacking the wireworm.

I wonder whether the minister would see to it that someone from the experimental farm inspects the small trees and vegetation roundabout these premises. I was looking at them the other day. They are being attacked, not by the fire blight but by something worse. The trouble will spread and valuable trees will be destroyed. I meant to telephone the Department of Agriculture but I did not know whom to get in touch with. Someone should be responsible because it is a very bad condition. It is at the back of this building, and the rapidity with which the destruction is going on is suoh that I should like to see it attended to at once. I bring it to the minister's attention in the hope that someone will look after it.

I am pleased that the leader of the opposition has called attention to it. Whenever the attention of the department is drawn to matters of this sort it has always 'been the practice to have an investigation made.
Who makes it?
It is made by this particular branch of the department.

Have there been any successful experiments in connection with the distribution by airplane of powder for the destruction of insects in western Canada this year?

Supply-Agriculture
Some preliminary work has been done particularly for forest insects, but it -has been found expensive to do it in that way; there are less expensive ways for field crop insects.

Item agreed to.
Salaries, $798,997.75; contingencies, $77,200.
There are three main reasons for the difference shown. The 1935-36 item for salaries is $711,334.25.
Will the minister give particulars of how this item is made up?

In a moment. First, I will give the main reasons for the difference and then I shall give the items, if necessary, from the itemized account. For 1936-37, the estimate is $798,997.75. There is an increase there of $87,663.50. If members of the committee will look at the next item, contingencies, it will be noted that the 1935-36 item is SI 14,200; the 1936-37 item is $77200; that is a decrease of $37,000. That decrease will be accounted for largely in the increase of $87,663 in the item for salaries. It is a transfer of salaries from contingencies into the civil government list.
There is still an increase of over $50,000.
I shall come to that in a moment. It is largely due to temporaries made permanent.
Was that $114,200 for contingencies all taken up last year?

Yes; it was all taken up last year. In addition to that there is the five per cent as compared with the former ten per cent deduction in salaries; there is five per cent added there. The balance is due to transfers of salaries from the branch votes to civil government.

Do I understand the minister to say that the-re have been no additions during the year to the staff of the Department of Agriculture; that none of this extra amount that is being voted is to be for new help?
There are twelve new stenographers.

There have been three new positions provided, but two of those are modified old ones. This does not mean the putting on of three individuals, but it is the creation of three new positions, two of them being modified old positions that were in existence before.
Will the minister say what those are?

The three of them are: the general executive assistant; that position has not been filled; it was created some time last year but it has not yet been filled; then there is the chief, fruit and vegetable field service, and the dominion agricultural chemist. The latter two were just modifications of previous positions.
And are they filled?
Yes; the latter two are filled.
Markets and transportation: two additions there, assistant chiefs.
Do I understand the hon. member to ask if those positions were in markets and transportation before?
No; are there not now two chief assistants in the markets and transportation branch?
In the fruit branch?
Yes.
The matter of appointments is under consideration.
They are provided for but not filled. At the bottom of page 70 of the estimates two of them are mentioned.
Field services, the same? The salaries are provided for.

They will be found all through the list. These were all in the branch votes. They were taken out of the branch votes and put into civil government this year. That is the only change there. If hon. members go over the items on pages 70, 71 and 72 of the estimates, they will find that this is shown there as an increase in civil government. That is the reason there are more of these employees.
An increase of fifty-four new employees?

Yes, but they are not
new employees. They are simply taken out of the branch votes we have already passed and put under civil government.
All except three.
All except three.

For instance, as regards
the four senior fruit and vegetable inspectors, they are not new creations? They are people whose salaries previously have been paid out of the particular vote?

Yes; that is my information.
Supply-Agriculture
Where does the increase of the $50,000 come from?

That increase is as shown. Part of it is due to the five per cent difference in salary deduction, and part of it is due to transfers from the branch votes into this vote for civil government. The $50,000 increase in the civil government vote is made up in that way, but it does not increase the total vote of the department by that amount.
Does it amount to this? At the top of page 71 of the estimates is one assistant chief, field services. I do not know if that is for fruit. Is it?
Yes.

His salary added to those of the four senior fruit and vegetable inspectors, makes $11,800, and that, I take it, if I understand the minister aright, is a set-up against the $15,600 deduction in the fruit vote.
In part it will be. There are other reasons, as I mentioned.

I note also that there is a
chief canning inspector whose office is being done away with at the present time. Perhaps I am going a little far afield in asking this question, though it has to do with the canning of fruits and vegetables. I understand that there is to be some change in the regulations respecting containers; that regulations are being prepared at the present time to standardize containers of fruits and vegetables after they are canned. Is such in contemplation? Are these regulations nearing completion? And what are they?

I understand that in
1933'the government established the practice whereby when a position was vacated it was allowed to lapse along with the vacation of the position. That move was made, I think, to cut down staffs in certain departments. It has been found necessary from time to time to reestablish some of these positions. This position went out of existence in that way, and will probably have to be reestablished to take care of the very matter that the hon. member has spoken of.

Yes, but I should like the
minister to give us the information for which I asked, regarding a change in the regulations for the standardization of containers for canned goods.

Really there has not
been any change up to date other than this, that I think it will be found that in the bill before the house there is a provision for a change in containers for cheese, packages for

cheese, and in connection with fruits. The matter of containers is under consideration as a result of the report made last year by the price spreads committee. The idea that at the moment is seemingly most acceptable to the department is that we might be well advised to depart from insistence upon certain weights in connection with canned fruits, accept the idea of volume and take pints, quarts, gallons and so on rather than deal with weights in the set-up of the packages. But the matter has not yet been fully decided, and no change has been definitely decided upon in connection with it.

May I ask the minister if
the department has received any representations from the canning industry as a whole, or from any of the larger concerns which are interested in canning, to the effect that they would rather have the net weight as the standard than the size of the container in quarts or pints or multiples of quarts or pints? I understand that they feel quite strongly on this matter, and that they are of the opinion that it is more in the interests of the canning industry, of the fruit farmer and of the vegetable farmer, that containers shall have the net weight marked distinctly on the package, so that the housewife may know what she is going to get. I should like to know if any representations have been made and any conferences held with respect to the matter.

Meetings and conferences have been held in that connection. I understand that one of the companies has expressed strong views with regard to the matter, believing that the net weight method is fairer than any other of providing containers. I believe that the other companies have open minds on the matter, some of them being favourable to containers in accordance with the view I expressed a moment ago, based upon pints and quarts and multiples of pints and quarts rather than upon weight.

I understand that one of the objections raised by one of the larger companies mentioned by the minister is that a certain quantity of goods is canned for export, and it has to conform to the regulations of the country to which it is to be exported. It is very difficult, of course, for these companies to estimate just how much they are going to be able to export, and if they overstep the mark and can a larger quantity than they are able to sell, in sizes that are required by the regulations of these foreign countries, a regulation which sets the size of the container in pints, quarts or multiples thereof would

Supply-Agriculture
make it impossible for the company to dispose in the domestic market of any goods which it was not able to export. I should like to ask the minister if all the companies have been consulted and if any conferences have been held.

Conferences have been held and, of course, all the companies will be consulted before anything final is done. The matter is under consideration at the moment, and the point raised by the hon. gentleman has been considered in a partial way but not finally determined. Nothing will be done that will interfere in any way with trade into any other country. We shall attempt to arrive at a conclusion that will make that kind of trade possible.
I think that is one instance where the Canadian Horticultural Council has demonstrated its usefulness.

I think in the main import countries require net weight to be shown. Within the British empire the standard is universal, but on the continent the metric system prevails, and there is some difficulty about weights. That is my information. I think the Department of Trade and Commerce should be consulted about this matter with a great deal of care, in relation to the reports from their trade commissioners. My information is that in the British empire we have a net weight standard, because we all have sixteen ounces to the pound. But once you get on the continent of Europe you have the metric system; the weight is indicated in grams and the volume in litres, which is an entirely different proposition. I should not think it would be a change for the better to provide quarts, pints and gallons as the standard to show the net amount the housewife is purchasing. I say that only because of some investigations I made in that connection in one of the large stores in London that dealt very largely with Canadian products. A standard which is known to be standard throughout the empire is one from which I think we should not depart unless we have the very best reasons for doing so.

I should like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that apparently about twelve extra stenographers have been taken on. Would the minister say that they were all taken from the temporary staff which he had last year?

I am informed that there is very little variation, if any, in the stenographic staff. Changes are made back and forth between the different branches; there
may be a cutting down in one and an increase in another, but as far as the total staff is concerned I am informed that it is practically the same as last year.
On page 72 of the estimates I see an increase from sixty to seventy-two stenographers under one item and from nineteen to twenty under another.

They are all covered by the explanation I gave a few moments ago. These are largely changes from the temporary staff to the permanent staff and from branch votes to the civil government vote. They are not increases in the number of individuals in the service.
That is with the exception of the three new positions, which have not been filled yet as I understand the situation.
No; they were on the staff and they have been transferred from one vote to another.
All but three?
There are just the three new positions.

I understood the minister to say that consideration was being given a question of changing containers for fruit. I should like to ask if the same consideration is being given containers for canned vegetables.

Yes. All the questions raised in connection with the price spreads investigation are being given consideration at the present time. There is only one on which we have reached a final decision, and that is still to be dealt with by the house in the legislation having to do with butter and cheese.

Would the minister explain
just what are the duties to be performed, by the general executive assistant?

That position was
created before I took over the department, and whoever was appointed was supposed to give general assistance to the executive in administering the affairs of the department, f have not found use for such an appointment up to date and I do not know that I shall, but we are making the vote now until the matter is finally determined.

Do not mention that; it might turn out to be another assistant chief electoral officer.
Supply-Agriculture
On page 71 of the estimates provision is made for a chief seed grader. What are his duties and does he work in the west or in the east?
He is in the executive office, the central office at Ottawa, but I am not in a position to give his duties in detail except that he will have charge over those who are grading seeds.

Before this item passes I should like to bring a certain condition to the attention of the minister, and I think it might come under the miscellaneous item. It has been the practice of the Department of Agriculture, in order to encourage and promote the distribution of pure seed, to pay the freight on all shipments of registered or certified seed made before March 2 of this year, under certain conditions which are set out. There have been brought to my attention certain cases in which it was impossible for the department to have the seed cleaned and ready for shipment before that date. When this matter was taken up with one of the seed stations the reply was that it was impossible to get the seed out under the free freight rate because it would not be ready for shipment by that date. In this particular instance the money for the seed grain had been sent to this station and was there for some time before the date fixed. The point is that the seed could not be shipped under free freight after that date, because it was not possible for the government to have it ready at that time, and also because the money was not voted for the following year to take care of this situation. I was wondering whether the minister would not consider what I have said when he is drawing up future estimates. That is to say, those who cannot take advantage of the free freight simply because of the inability of the department to have the seed ready in time are subjected to extra expense. I believe it is unfair to ask the farmer to bear that extra cost. It would be good policy for the government to set aside a very small sum-it would not need to be large-to take care of these cases, and I believe it would be easy for the department to find out how many such cases there have been in the last few years and to base their estimates upon the facts as they have gathered them. I speak to the point because some farmers obtain the benefit of the free freight rate, while others, through no fault of their own, but because the government cannot get the seed out in time, are forced to pay freight. Between the free freight date and the time new moneys are voted to provide

for the item in the next year, I suggest that some provision should be made to take care of the farmers who do not receive the free freight rate.

The letter sent out may be open to a wrong interpretation. It is generally known that the end of the financial years is on March 31. These votes cover the year from April 1 until March 31 of the following year. Most farmers who are laying in seed for the spring have obtained it before the end of March. That is the common practice throughout Canada and the practice of those who are providing themselves with the amount of seed indicated in the vote. There have been cases where people have not had their applications in sufficiently early. If the applications were not in about the middle of February it is possible that delivery of the seed could not be made in sufficient time to get it out before the vote lapses. But in actual practice most of those accounts have been paid. All those cases are subject to review, and when the new votes come in on April 1, the moneys are used to take care of cases which have been carried over from the previous year. However, in order to protect themselves against conditions which might arise, officials of the department necessarily send out orders from year to year to get applications sufficiently early to make it possible for delivery early in the month of March. I believe the letter could be interpreted as more or less a warning to a man to get his order in earlier next year.

The seed growers' association and organization take the responsibility for sending out advice of this kind to the farmers, and perhaps when they are notifying farmers of seed price lists they could send a notice to the effect that it would be much better for them if they had their orders in before a certain date. If February 1 is a date satisfactory to all concerned I believe it would be a good idea to include that information in the pamphlets sent out.
We shall consider the suggestion.

When the minister replied to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) stating the reason for the increase in salaries, he said that it was due partly to transfers from the temporary to the permanent list, and partly to statutory increases. It would seem that $37,000 would refer to transfers, and we would assume that $50,000 was required to cover statutory increases.

Some of the $50,000 is paid in connection with the transfer of

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
individuals from one vote to another, as well as from contingencies, in addition to the amount which would be necessary to pay the statutory increases.

I do not wish to transgress the rules of the house, but I think the minister will recall that when one of the first votes was passed I asked that one vote be left so that anything concerning the estimates might be discussed. May I ask the minister if the government has made a final decision against aonusing cheese this year?
That would come under the next item.

Item agreed to.
Natural Products Marketing Act, 1934, $106,000.

Last year there was a vote of $1,545,500, and this year the vote is $106,600. The difference in the two items is due to the cheese bonus and the amount expended last year in connection with the export marketing of butter. As was announced, the- government has decided not to pay the cheese bonus this year.

In connection with the marketing of our natural products there are some observations I should like to make to the minister. I realize that perhaps one of the most serious problems which will face us within the next years is that of marketing our natural products, and particularly our agricultural products. I have no use for finding fault without offering some kind of solution. Where the difficulty is obvious to everyone, and no solution is offered, discussion seems idle, but I believe what I have to say might help at least to some degree to solve the problem we must face. It is recognized that agriculture must continue as Canada's basic industry, and it is also recognized that that industry is suffering. There are many causes for anxiety; for example, a large crop of wheat, an overproduction of meat products, or of butter, or of potatoes, may cause us great concern, and sooner or later we must find a solution for our difficulty. We are attempting to solve the problem. This item for the bonusing of chee j is a good example of that. We are pegging prices for wheat and we shall peg other prices, I fancy. We have a marketing act now before the courts, and I am quite sure that we shall put through another marketing act if the present one is not upheld by the courts. We have a Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, which is a most excellent one, and for which I desire to commend
everyone who had any part in bringing it in. It will be followed by others of its kind, I assume.
There are two problems, however, to which I think we have not thus far given sufficient attention in Canada, and the time is now ripe to give attention to them. One is the maintenance of soil fertility. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act attempted something along that line, glancing at the soil drifting difficulties which have arisen in different parts of Canada. We have another serious question which we must face before long, and that is the problem of the economic use of irrigated land. I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the committee, but I wish all members of the committee could be out for a little while in the constituency I represent. There are four distinct irrigation projects there, and they are, to use the fine description which the bon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) applied to the Canadian National Railways, a magnificent asset. I feel that one is perfectly justified in applying that term to them, and it is an asset whose value I believe can be greatly increased to the great advantage of this country. But before that can be done we must look to the economic use of these projects or we shall have a magnificent asset turning, because we misuse it, to our disadvantage.
Having said this much, I wish now to direct the attention of the minister to the condition of the beet sugar industry in Canada. I would ask all members of this committee to give their earnest consideration to the condition of the beet sugar industry because there are at present many misunderstandings and misconceptions about it, and it is very easy to make a grave mistake in connection with it. The minister might possibly have overlooked some facts in connection with this industry which, I think, should be brought to his attention, and by the way may I say without his feeling that I am endeavouring to flatter him that I have a very high opinion of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I feel that he is the right man in the right place, but with the multiplicity of his duties it would be an easy matter for him not to have given a matter of this kind particular attention. There are also, I believe, many members of this committee who, because they do not come from territory similar to that in my constituency do not realize what irrigation project districts are like, just as I myself, when I had occasion to go through part of Quebec a little while ago, found that I could never have imagined what the actual conditions were like in that province without going there. I am quite sure that some

3466	COMMONS
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
members of this committee cannot imagine what conditions are like in the irrigated regions without going there and seeing for themselves, and I should like to help them see something of the nature of these projects.
The problem of the beet sugar industry is a difficult one, much more difficult than most people in this country .realize. We are at the present time placing a levy on the beet sugar industry.	We are bonusing wheat,
bonusing cheese, and aiding in various ways a good many other industries in Canada, but on the beet sugar industry we are placing a handicap, and this will show how serious that handicap is: The government tax, the one cent levy on each pound of sugar produced, was so grievous that it amounted in 1935 to 54-7 per cent of the gross returns to the farmer. I do not believe anyone could have imagined that the government got 54-7 per cent of what the farmer got for every ton of beets delivered to the factory. That is an unjust situation, I am sure. Again, the government, through this levy, received 66 per cent more than the labourers received who did the work on the beets.

That would cover all
the municipal, provincial and federal taxes?

No; that is just the dominion tax. I wish, Mr. Chairman, with your permission to put on Hansard some figures which are right up to date and have come from the Raymond sugar factory, which is a very accurate one, to illustrate the handicap under which the beet sugar industry carries on. The government is receiving so much money from the beet sugar industry that it receives on an average, clear, 13-6 times as much money as the farmer receives on an average, clear, per ton of beets. This is an almost inconceivable, an almost unbelievable situation; yet it is borne out by the figures I shall presently put on Hansard.	_
There is another point, and that is that Canada is, so far as I have been able to learn, the only country in which there is not definite assistance given to the sugar beet industry. Canada, on the contrary, actually places a oandicap on that industry.
May I ask a question? Mr. BLACKMORE: If it does not require me to digress too much.

I wonder whether the
hon. member would amplify his statement that the dominion government receives thirteen times as much as the sugar beet farmer.

What is the government tax?
Mr. BLACIvMORE: One cent per pound excise tax. The gross average amount received per grower was SI,018.86, and the gross average cost of production per grower was 8978.07 The net average profit per grower was 840.79

Do the growers pay this one cent tax? The consumers claim that they pay it.
Mr. BLACIvMORE: I am glad that point has been brought up.
The consumers claim that they would be able to get sugar one cent per pound cheaper if it were not for this tax.
When the farmer delivers his beets to the sugar company they tell him that they would be able to pay more if they did not have to pay this tax.
They charge the tax.

In any case the farmer has to pay the tax. We shall go on. The average amount of the government tax per grower is 8558.48. For every dollar paid out in labour during the beet crop, the government receives $1.66. I have not the time, nor would it be fair to take up the time to go into these figures, but I think it worth while to put them on Hansard so that hon. members who are interested can study them. One or two hon. members would seem to be inclined to scoff just a little, but I think it would be well if the} would consider these figures very carefully before they say much. Otherwise, they might not feel very proud of what they do say.
I should like to draw to the attention of the committee the national need of a beet sugar industry at the present time. Unemployment is our most serious difficulty, but it has been estimated in the United States that for every factory of 1,200 tons' capacity, 10.000 people would be employed. That is a surprising estimate and I should like to read something to bear it out. Let me quote from a pamphlet entitled, Why Canada Needs Sugar Beets, by the joint sugar beet development committee. Lethbridge, Alberta. I read from page 16:
It has been estimated in the United States that one factory of from 1,000 to 1,200 daily capacity will, directly and indirectly, give a living to 10,000 people-men, women, and children.
12739-221 i
There is another statement which appears on page 19 of the same pamphlet:
Mr. Charles H. Houston, president of the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company, when appearing as a witness before the select standing committee of the Canadian House of Commons inquiring into the beet sugar industry. made the following significant statement: "I will say this, that the beet sugar industry employs a tremendous amount of labour. There is no other industry that I know that takes care of as much labour as the beet industry."
I should like to quote from an article by S. P. Grounds which appeared in the October, 1931, number of Empire Production, published in London, England, as follows:
It is undoubtedly in the direction of increasing home supplies of sugar that the industry in Canada will continue to develop. The prairie provinces themselves have been computed to import sugar worth $10,000,000 every year. This might well be supplied by six or seven more factories like that at Raymond, cultivating 60.000 to 75,000 acres, giving employment to 5,000 farmers, 8,000 hand labourers and 2,000 factory workers, and utilizing each year 125.000 tons of coal,
1.500.000	sugar bags. 30,000 tons of limerock,
3.000	tons of coke, 200 tons of soda ash, and large supplies of other materials.
I direct the attention of hon. members of the committee to the number of acres which could be taken out of wheat production. This article indicates the possibilities in the beet sugar industry, but I am afraid that so far these have been neglected in Canada.
Might I ask a question of the hon. gentleman?

I speak very seldom in committee, and I crave your indulgence, Mr. Chairman, for probably five or ten minutes. I have the honour to represent what is probably the largest district devoted to the beet growing industry in Ontario, and I feel I would be remiss in my duty if I did not for a moment or two speak on this subject. Since I came to Ottawa I have probably heard more talk about the tariff on sugar, .-and the protection given beets destroying the potato industry in the maritime provinces, than anything else. I wondered whether that was the case. I found that Canada has a :trade agreement with Great Britain, and with .the British West Indies, which is a British [DOT]possession, as regards a duty on sugar.
They are separate. The treaty with the West Indies was long prior to the 1932 agreement.
At the present time there is a stated duty which, I believe, cannot be changed before 1937, and even then not without twelve months' notice. About that time, in 1931 or 1932-
No; it was prior to that. The agreement was made not under the late government, but under the government that preceded it.

About 1932 I believe that very cheap sugar was being dumped into Canada. At that time a dump duty was put on refined sugar coming into this country. It was imposed at the request not of the beet-growing industry, but, probably, of the sugar refineries; possibly the competition was unfair; I do not know.
It was Cuban sugar that came in.

Cuba is not in quite the same position to-day. Because of a special trade agreement with the United *States, that island is selling two-thirds of her products to the United States at what is, for sugar, a very fair price. The other one-third she is dumping, mostly into Great Britain, at
I Mr. Blackmore.]
a very cheap rate. Great Britain has imposed or is about to impose a dump duty upon all sugar that is selling below SI .75 per hundredweight. The sugar beet industry and the consumption of beet sugar have increased marvellously during the last few years. Fifty years ago not more than ten per cent of the world's sugar was beet sugar. To-day almost forty per cent of the world's consumption of sugar is of beet sugar. Great Britain and the United States, which have been large importers of sugar, are to-day growing from twenty to twenty-five per cent of their own sugar as beet sugar.
In 1903 or about that time the beet sugar industry was started in Canada. It made fairly rapid progress until about 1920, when the great sugar debacle of that year ruined a great many of the organizations that were insecurely grounded. Now, in 1936, we have again some thriving sugar beet factories. In the riding I represent, at Wallaceburg they are refining beet sugar at the rate of a hundred tons of raw pulp an hour, or twenty-four hundred tons a day.
For how many months?
For probably three months.
The important thing is the number of months.

In spite of that dump duty Canada imports approximately eighty-four per cent of the sugar she consumes. The average consumption of sugar in this country is quite heavy. I think it is ninety pounds per capita or more.
Eighty pounds.

It varies from one year to another. The amount of excise that is collected on sugar has already been mentioned by my hon. friend. I got it from the bureau of statistics, and I assume it is correct. The excise collected on sugar for the year 1934-35 was $11,037,278. Import duties collected on the sugar we imported for the fiscal year were: not above Dutch standard, $3,433,000; sugar above Dutch standard, $1,373,000, or a total duty, collected on sugar we imported, of approximately $4,807,000, which, added to excise of $11,037,278, makes a total levy of $15,844,322 on sugar consumed in Canada. In spite of that heavy tax on sugar, this product is selling more cheaply to-day than at any time in our history. I was passing through London a week or two ago when sugar was retailing at $4.80 a hundred pounds. Take off your excise, which surely

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
has nothing to do with the cost, and you have sugar selling to-day on the market at S3.80 per hundred pounds.
The duty was reduced last year to one cent a pound.
That is what I say; take off the one cent per pound and your sugar costs the consumer to-day, without that tax, $3.80 a hundred pounds.
Retail.
Retail, yes. It retails at $4.80, and taking off the excise it is really retailing at $3.80, the cheapest price at which sugar has been sold in the history of Canada.
Those figures are computed on the two cent basis, rather than, as the right hon. gentleman points out, one cent.

No, they are not. I took the one cent rate. There is nothing new about the sugar industry. Hon. members who sat here in 1932 and 1933 can remember that, on February 24, 1932, after an exhaustive and careful investigation of the situation, the select committee on agriculture and colonization submitted this report:
Your committee, therefore, recommends that in view of the existing tariff on sugar and in consideration of the substantial payments being made to agriculture and labour by the beet sugar factories at present in operation, the cane sugar refineries should undertake to provide for a gradual increase of factory facilities for the refining of beet sugar in Canada, and that with the additional advantages in freight rates to points in the middle west, heretofore described, factory facilities should now be steadily increased in western areas where beets are grown, and thereby make it possible to produce from beets a more substantial percentage of the sugar consumption of Canada.
There is something further I should like to say that should be rather interesting, for I cannot help thinking that these countries which produce beet sugar cannot all be wrong. I believe beet sugar has a future in Canada. M. Golodetz, an authority on sugar, writing in the weekly Sugar Market Review of recent date, says that existing rates of duty on raw and refined sugar offer very inadequate protection to the sugar beet industry, particularly when we bear in mind that the cane production has been and is very substantially subsidized. Nearly all of what is known as the world's production is protected. He points out that over ninety per cent of the sugar for the world's sugar market is produced and marketed under various forms of state protection. Moreover, cane is produced under labour conditions that do not bear comparison with those of
Canadian labour. Sufficient it is to say that as a Canadian people we cannot entertain the lowering of the present level of labour but should rather strive to raise the present standard.
The other day in this house we spent a good deal of time in discussing the possibilities and the future of the soya bean industry in Canada. The farmers of this country have a great deal of money invested in beet sugar equipment. They have imported trained men from other countries who have become naturalized Canadians, and I think it would be a mistake to have the beet sugar industry forced out of business. I feel sure that if that result were brought about the companies which are subsidized would raise the price of sugar once they got rid of that competition, so in the long run we would have to pay more for our sugar. I do not want our friends from the maritime provinces to think we are trying to steal their markets. I believe there is a place for both beets and potatoes in this dominion, and I think we would do well to devote a great deal of study to this question, because Canada with its great resources will support a very much larger beet sugar industry than we have at the present. Certainly I have no hesitation in urging that the one cent tax in so far as beet sugar is concerned should be removed.

I should like to ask the minister a question, but first I should like to compliment the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) on the interesting address he gave us. It was one of the most instructive and practical speeches I have heard from his group. I can understand the hon. gentleman far better when he talks about beets and acres and cents than when he talks about just prices and dividends. I hope he will enlarge his activities along the line he took to-night; I am sure we would all profit by it.
This vote shows, according to the minister, a large reduction due to our ceasing to bonus cheese. Could the minister indicate why that has been done? Was it not satisfactory or have conditions so changed as to render it no longer necessary?
That would seem to be temporary.

It may be temporary, but these figures can hardly be explained in that way. There is another reason; the price is very much better at the present time than it was a year ago. Not only is it better in the United States market; it is better in the British market as well. Then there are understandings in connection with trade treaties with different countries that may be interfered with by the payment of bonuses. We in Canada as a people took exception to certain activities in countries such as Australia in connection with state encouragement of the production of butter. Probably we might expect other countries to take the same exception to similar action on our part if we have trade arrangements with them.
No exception was taken by any country, was it?

Not directly, but there was an indication that some exception might

be taken. Questions were asked with regard to the matter.
Would not the United States automatically increase the duty by the amount of the bonus?

They have not said so, but there have been inquiries as to what were our intentions. Those came after we had made our decision, as a matter of fact; the decision was not the result of any threats or anything like that, but such inquiries have been made. All matters having been taken into consideration, we are of opinion that we can benefit both the butter industry and the cheese industry in Canada to a greater extent by providing markets and assisting in the maintenance and further development of those markets rather than by encouraging a greater production without any special market being provided for it. We think probably more can be done in the - way I have mentioned, and I believe our experience in regard to the United States trade treaty indicates our view to be sound. Our greater exportations of cheese to the United States and Great Britain have had something to do with the better price that we are getting for cheese at the present time, and as compared with last year that price per pound is greater than the amount of the bonus that was being paid.
I should like to have something to say in regard to this matter-
